title: TypeScript
blurb: Structural typing, narrowing, generics, and the boundary where types stop being guarantees. Nearly every JS role now screens on this.

questions.q: What is the difference between `any` and `unknown`?
choices: `unknown` switches off checking; `any` accepts anything but must be narrowed first
`any` is erased at compile time, while `unknown` survives as a runtime type check
`any` switches off checking; `unknown` accepts anything but must be narrowed first
They behave the same; `unknown` is simply the name that newer lint rules prefer
questions.why: `any` is contagious: everything derived from it is unchecked too. `unknown` is the safe top type: you can assign anything to it, but you cannot call, index or read it until you narrow it. Neither survives compilation, so the 'runtime check' option is wrong.
questions.asked: The clearest signal of whether someone uses TypeScript or just tolerates it.

questions.q: Does TypeScript check types at runtime?
choices: No: types are erased at compile time, so nothing is checked when the code runs
Partly: interfaces are erased, but type aliases are kept for `instanceof` checks
Yes: the emitted JavaScript keeps type checks at every function boundary
Only in development builds, where the bundler injects runtime assertions
questions.why: Type annotations are stripped from the output. That is why `typeof` and `instanceof` are the runtime tools, why you cannot `switch` on a type, and why data crossing the network needs real validation rather than an annotation.
questions.asked: It sets up the follow-up that matters: how do you validate an API response, then?

questions.q: What is wrong with this line?
questions.code: const user = await (await fetch('/api/me')).json() as User;
choices: `as` cannot be applied to an awaited expression, so this fails to compile
Nothing: `json()` is generic, so `as User` just fills in its type argument
Nothing: `fetch` rejects a body that does not match the declared type
`as` asserts without checking, so a changed API shape goes unnoticed
questions.why: `json()` returns `Promise<any>`; `as User` tells the compiler to stop asking and nothing verifies the shape. `fetch` knows nothing about your types. Validate at the boundary with a schema library or a hand-written type guard.
questions.asked: The single most valuable TypeScript question for a CRUD role: it separates typed code from checked data.

questions.q: What is the type of `config.port` here?
questions.code:
type Config = { mode: 'dark' | 'light'; port: string | number };
const config = { mode: 'dark', port: 8080 } satisfies Config;
choices: `string | number`, because `satisfies` applies the declared type
`number`, because `satisfies` checks but keeps the inferred type
`any`, because `satisfies` only runs its check at runtime
`8080`, because `satisfies` makes every property a literal
questions.why: `satisfies` errors if the object does not fit `Config`, but the variable keeps its own inferred type, so `config.port` is `number` and `toFixed` works without narrowing. An annotation (`const config: Config`) would widen it to `string | number`; `as` would not check it at all.
questions.asked: A newer operator, so it signals whether someone keeps current, and it tests the annotation-versus-inference distinction.

questions.q: What is a discriminated union?
choices: A union of primitive types that the compiler sorts from widest to narrowest
A union of object types sharing a literal tag field the compiler narrows on
A union with `null` and `undefined` removed by the `NonNullable` helper
An interface whose optional fields are checked by a runtime discriminator
questions.why: `{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error'; error: Error } | { status: 'ok'; data: T }`. Checking `state.status === 'ok'` narrows the whole object, so `state.data` exists only where it can. Optional fields cannot give you that guarantee.
questions.asked: Describe this well and you have effectively answered 'how do you model loading states?' too.

questions.q: How do you make a `switch` over a union exhaustive, so a new member breaks the build?
choices: Add `default: break` so any unhandled member falls through quietly
Enable `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, which checks every union member
Replace the `switch` with `if`/`else`, which the compiler checks fully
Assign the value to a `never` variable in the `default` branch
questions.why: `default: { const _exhaustive: never = value; throw new Error(...) }`. When someone adds a union member, that assignment stops compiling at every switch that forgot it. `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` only stops cases running into each other; it says nothing about missing members.
questions.asked: It shows you use the type system as a refactoring safety net, which is the real pitch for TypeScript.

questions.q: Is TypeScript structurally or nominally typed?
choices: Structurally: compatibility is decided by shape, not by the declared name
Nominally: two types are related only if one is declared to extend the other
Nominally, unless a class opts in to structural checks with `implements`
It depends on the tsconfig: `strict` switches the checker to nominal typing
questions.why: Any object with the right properties satisfies an interface, even if it never declared it. That is why a `UserId` and an `OrderId` that are both `string` are interchangeable, and why branded types exist. The exception: a class with `private`, `protected` or `#` members is compatible only with its own lineage.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'so how would you stop two string ids being swapped?', which leads to branded types.

questions.q: What is a branded type and why use one?
choices: A type imported from a specific npm package, so its origin is tracked
A type alias exported from its own module so it cannot be recreated
A primitive intersected with a unique marker, so distinct ids cannot be swapped
A type alias with a JSDoc tag that the compiler enforces on each call site
questions.why: `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }`. Passing an `OrderId` where a `UserId` is expected now fails to compile, though both are strings at runtime. A type alias from its own module is still just `string` structurally. It costs one cast where ids are created.
questions.asked: It comes up as 'how would you stop someone passing the wrong id?', a real bug class in CRUD code.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `interface` and `type`?
choices: Interfaces are for classes and emit a runtime object; type aliases are erased
Type aliases merge when re-declared; only interfaces can express unions and tuples
Type aliases are the legacy form and are deprecated in favour of interfaces
Interfaces merge when re-declared; only type aliases can express unions and tuples
questions.why: Declaration merging matters when augmenting a library's types. Type aliases are the only way to write a union, a conditional type or a template literal type. Neither emits runtime code. For a plain object shape, either works: pick one and be consistent.
questions.asked: A guaranteed question. The weak answer is 'interfaces are for classes'.

questions.q: What does `strictNullChecks` change?
choices: `null` becomes a compile error anywhere, so optional values must use `undefined`
The compiler inserts runtime null checks before every property access it emits
`null` and `undefined` stop being assignable to every type, so absence is explicit
Only function parameters are checked for null; locals and fields stay unchecked
questions.why: Without it, `string` silently includes `null`, so the compiler cannot warn you. With it you write `string | null` where absence is real, and the compiler forces a check before use. It emits no runtime code; it is the highest-value flag in the config.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know what `strict` actually buys you, rather than treating it as a magic switch.

questions.q: What is the difference between `foo?: string` and `foo: string | undefined`?
choices: The optional form also accepts `null`; the union form accepts only `undefined`
The union form must be present, possibly `undefined`; the optional one may be omitted
They are identical, and the compiler rewrites one into the other when it checks
The optional form must be present but may be `undefined`; the union may be omitted
questions.why: `?:` means the key may be absent; the union means the key is required but its value may be `undefined`. In a PATCH, 'key absent' means leave alone, and on the wire 'clear it' must be `null` because JSON drops `undefined`. The distinction matters in-process, and sharpens under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.
questions.asked: A precise question that maps onto a real API design decision: how a PATCH says 'leave alone' versus 'clear'.

questions.q: What does `B` resolve to?
questions.code:
type A = { id: number; name: string };
type B = Omit<A, 'name'> & { name: number };
choices: { id: number; name: number }
{ id: number; name: string & number }
{ id: number; name: string | number }
{ id: number }
questions.why: `Omit` removes `name` first, so the intersection adds it back with the new type. Without the `Omit`, `name` would be `string & number`, which is `never`. This is the standard idiom for overriding one field of an existing type.
questions.asked: It is the idiom behind most DTO types, so it shows whether you can read everyday type code.

questions.q: What does `Partial<T>` do?
choices: Makes every property of `T` readonly
Removes `undefined` from each property of `T`
Makes every property of `T` optional
Makes every nested property of `T` optional
questions.why: It is useful for a PATCH payload or an options object; its counterpart is `Required<T>`. It is shallow: nested objects keep their required fields, so it is not a deep partial.
questions.asked: A warm-up that often leads into 'how would you type a PATCH body?'.

questions.q: When is a generic type parameter actually needed?
choices: When the input and output types must stay related to each other
Whenever a function accepts an object argument of any kind
Always, as the type-safe way to avoid writing `any` in a signature
Only in published library code, never in application code
questions.why: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` carries the element type through. A type parameter used once and related to nothing else adds no safety over `unknown`; it is `any` with extra syntax.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check whether generics are understood or cargo-culted.

questions.q: What does `Keys` resolve to?
questions.code: type Keys = keyof { id: number; name: string };
choices: string
['id', 'name']
number | string
'id' | 'name'
questions.why: `keyof` gives a union of the literal key types, not a tuple and not the value types. Combined with a constraint it gives a type-safe getter: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.
questions.asked: The `get` function built on it is one of the most common TypeScript live-coding exercises.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: The callback parameter `s` needs an explicit `string` annotation
`map` does not exist on `string`, so the union must be narrowed
A union of a type and its own array type is not allowed
`trim` is not available on the elements of a union array
questions.why: On a union you can only use members present on every branch, and `string` has no `map`. Narrow with `Array.isArray(input)` first, or normalise the input to an array at the top of the function.
questions.asked: It checks that you read compiler errors on unions as 'narrow first', not as 'add a cast'.

questions.q: What is a user-defined type guard?
choices: A decorator that validates a parameter before the method body runs
A function returning `arg is Type`, which narrows the argument for the caller
A compiler flag that inserts `typeof` checks at every function boundary
A cast written as `<Type>arg`, the older syntax for an `as` assertion
questions.why: `function isUser(v: unknown): v is User { ... }`. The compiler trusts the signature, so the body has to really check; a lazy guard is an `as` with more steps.
questions.asked: The follow-up is 'what happens if the guard's body is wrong?', which tests whether you know the compiler trusts it blindly.

questions.q: Given `const cfg: { readonly port: number } = load()`, what does `readonly` stop?
choices: Any change to `port` at runtime, because the object is frozen on creation
Reads of `port` outside the module that declared the type
Assignment to `port` and to every nested property below it
Assignment to `port` through `cfg`, at compile time only
questions.why: Types are erased, so `readonly` only stops writes through that type during compilation; another alias without `readonly` can still mutate the object. It is also shallow. `Object.freeze` is the runtime tool, and it is shallow too.
questions.asked: It separates people who know types are erased from people who think the compiler protects the running program.

questions.q: What type does `routes` get?
questions.code: const routes = ['home', 'about'] as const;
choices: readonly ['home', 'about']
string[], with the array frozen at runtime
('home' | 'about')[]
readonly string[]
questions.why: `as const` infers the narrowest literal types and makes the result readonly, so this is a readonly tuple of literals. It does nothing at runtime. With it you can derive a union: `type Route = typeof routes[number]`, which is `'home' | 'about'`.
questions.asked: A very practical trick: one source of truth for both a runtime list and a type.

questions.q: For a status field sent to and from a JSON API, why do many teams prefer a string-literal union over an `enum`?
choices: An enum is not type-safe, because any string can be assigned to one
A union is faster at runtime, because enum lookups go through an object
A union erases completely and matches the JSON values you actually send
An enum cannot be used in a `switch`, so exhaustiveness checks fail
questions.why: A union of `'draft' | 'published'` emits no code and is exactly the JSON on the wire. A regular enum emits a runtime object, string enums reject the raw string from JSON without a cast, and numeric enums serialise as numbers. Enums do work in `switch`; that option is simply false.
questions.asked: An 'explain your preference' question: either choice is defensible if you can name the trade-off.

questions.q: What is the type of `config.mode`?
questions.code: const config = { retries: 3, mode: 'dark' };
choices: 'dark'
any
readonly 'dark'
string
questions.why: Properties of an object literal are mutable, so they widen to their base type: you could assign `config.mode = 'light'` later. `as const`, or a contextual type with a literal union, keeps the literal.
questions.asked: It explains the common 'Type string is not assignable to type "dark" | "light"' error that juniors hit daily.

questions.q: What is the `Result` pattern and why use it instead of throwing?
choices: A helper that retries a failing call and returns its final outcome
A wrapper that converts any thrown exception into a `null` return value
Returning `{ ok, value } | { ok, error }` so failure appears in the type
A replacement for every try/catch, including for programming errors
questions.why: A thrown error is invisible to the type system; nothing forces a caller to handle it. A Result puts the failure path in the signature. It is verbose, so most codebases use it for expected failures and still throw for bugs, which is why 'replace every try/catch' is wrong.
questions.asked: A design-opinion question that maps onto the same exceptions-versus-Result debate in C#.

questions.q: What does the `!` do here?
questions.code: const el = document.getElementById('root')!;
choices: It throws a descriptive error at runtime if the element is missing
It removes `null` from the type, with no check when the code runs
It converts a `null` result into `undefined` for optional chaining
It waits for the element to exist before returning it to the caller
questions.why: It is `as NonNullable<T>` in one character and emits nothing. Fine where you genuinely know more than the compiler, but `if (!el) throw new Error('#root is missing')` gives a real error message instead of a later 'cannot read properties of null'.
questions.asked: Reviewers flag `!` constantly; knowing when it is a lie is the point.

questions.q: What does `Record<'draft' | 'live', number>` require?
choices: An object with both `draft` and `live` keys, each holding a number
An array of two numbers indexed by the strings `'draft'` and `'live'`
An object with a `draft` or a `live` key, whose value is a number
An object with any string keys, as long as every value is a number
questions.why: With a union of literal keys, `Record` requires every key, so a lookup table fails to compile when the union grows and nobody adds the new entry. `Record<string, number>` is the open-ended dictionary form.
questions.asked: It leads into using the compiler to keep lookup tables complete as a union grows.

questions.q: Why can this crash at runtime although it compiles under `strict`?
choices: `strict` turns index reads into `any`, so `user` is no longer checked
`Record` is erased, so `map[id]` returns the whole object at runtime
Indexing is typed `User` even when the key is missing from the object
`id` might be a number, and numeric keys are not stored in a Record
questions.why: By default TypeScript assumes any index into a record or array succeeds. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (not part of `strict`) adds `| undefined` to every index access and forces a check: noisier, but it catches real crashes.
questions.asked: A strong signal: it shows you have tuned a tsconfig rather than accepted the defaults.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` at each `return`?
choices: string at the first, number at the second
string | number at both returns
string at the first, string | number at the second
string at the first, unknown at the second
questions.why: Control-flow analysis narrows inside the branch and also narrows the rest of the function by elimination, because the string case has already returned. That is why an early return is often the cleanest way to narrow.
questions.asked: It checks that you know narrowing continues after an early return, which shapes how you write guards.

questions.q: What is the `never` type used for?
choices: Marking APIs as deprecated so the editor strikes through each call site
Typing a function that returns nothing, as another spelling of `void`
Typing a value that is always `null`, such as a cleared field
Exhaustiveness checks, and functions that always throw or never return
questions.why: `never` has no values: nothing is assignable to it, which is what makes the exhaustive-switch trick work. A function that always throws is inferred as returning `never`. `void` is different: the function returns, just with nothing useful.
questions.asked: It checks you can explain the exhaustive-switch trick rather than copy it.

questions.q: Why does `items.forEach(x => set.add(x))` type-check, when `set.add` returns the Set?
choices: `forEach` is typed with `any` for the callback's return value
A callback typed `() => void` may return anything; it is ignored
Arrow functions with one expression are always inferred as `void`
The compiler inserts a `return undefined` into inline callbacks
questions.why: Assigning a function to a `void`-returning function type deliberately allows any return value, because the caller promises to ignore it. A callback type returning `undefined` would reject `set.add`. The arrow itself still infers `Set<number>`; nothing is rewritten.
questions.asked: An edge case that explains why `void` and `undefined` are not interchangeable as return types.

questions.q: Which signature types a getter that returns the property's own type?
choices: `function get(obj: object, key: string): any`
`function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`
`function get<T>(obj: T, key: string): T`
`function get(obj: Record<string, unknown>, key: string): unknown`
questions.why: The constraint ties the key to the object and the indexed access type ties the return to the key, so `get(user, 'name')` is `string` and `get(user, 'nope')` fails to compile. The `unknown` version is safe but forces a cast at every call.
questions.asked: The canonical 'write me a generic' exercise.

questions.q: What does `Pick<T, K>` do, and what is its opposite?
choices: It makes keys `K` optional; `Required<T, K>` reverses it
It extracts union members `K`; `Exclude<T, K>` drops them
It keeps the first `K` keys; `Drop<T, K>` removes them
It keeps only keys `K`; `Omit<T, K>` removes them instead
questions.why: Both derive a DTO from a domain model, e.g. `type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>`. `Extract`/`Exclude` work on union members, not object keys. Note that with `Omit`, a sensitive field added later is included by default; `Pick` is the safer allow-list.
questions.asked: It usually leads to 'which is safer for a public DTO?', where Pick's allow-list wins.

questions.q: Under `strict`, what happens with this code?
choices: It compiles, and a non-Dog ends up inside `dogs`
A compile error on the assignment `animals = dogs`
A compile error on the `push`, which lacks `breed`
It compiles, then `push` throws a runtime TypeError
questions.why: Arrays are covariant in TypeScript for ergonomics, so `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]`, and pushing an `Animal` through that alias is allowed. The result is unsound: `dogs` now holds an object with no `breed`, and nothing throws. Type a parameter you only read from as `readonly Animal[]`, which has no `push`.
questions.asked: A deep-end question: knowing the hole exists is worth more than being able to name 'covariance'.

questions.q: What is the safest way to type a JSON payload whose shape you do not control?
choices: Type it as `any` and read fields directly, since JSON has no methods
Cast it with `as` to the interface the API documentation describes
Type it as `unknown`, then validate it with a schema or a type guard
Wrap every property access in try/catch so a bad shape cannot crash
questions.why: Validation is the only thing that turns runtime data into a type you can trust. Libraries like Zod derive the static type from the runtime schema, so the two cannot drift. A cast trusts the documentation, which is exactly what goes stale.
questions.asked: The practical heart of TypeScript in a CRUD app.

questions.q: What does 'make impossible states unrepresentable' mean?
choices: Throwing early whenever a function receives a combination of invalid inputs
Marking every field `readonly` so no code can put an object in a bad state
Validating every form in the UI layer so bad states never reach the server
Modelling types so that contradictory combinations cannot be constructed
questions.why: `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: Error }` permits loading, errored and loaded at once. A discriminated union permits exactly three states, so half the defensive code disappears. Throwing and validating handle bad states at runtime; this prevents them at compile time.
questions.asked: Using the phrase correctly signals real type-design experience.

questions.q: What does a `.d.ts` file contain?
choices: The compiled JavaScript output, minified for publishing to npm
Default compiler options that a tsconfig can inherit from
Type declarations only, describing code that exists elsewhere
Documentation comments extracted for the editor's hover text
questions.why: Declaration files hold ambient types with no runtime code. They are how `@types/*` packages describe untyped libraries, and how you declare globals or module augmentations in your own project. Shared compiler options live in a base tsconfig reached through `extends`.
questions.asked: It comes up when a library has no types, and the follow-up is 'what would you do about it?'.

questions.q: What does `Handler` resolve to?
questions.code: type Handler = `on${Capitalize<'click' | 'focus'>}`;
choices: 'on' | 'Click' | 'Focus'
'onClick' | 'onFocus'
`on${'click' | 'focus'}`
`on${string}`
questions.why: Template literal types distribute over unions and compose with the intrinsic string types (`Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`). Handy for deriving prop names or route params from a string.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can read the type-level string tricks that libraries like routers use.

questions.q: Why is `error` typed `unknown` in this catch clause under `strict`?
questions.code: try { /* ... */ } catch (error) { }
choices: Because JavaScript can throw any value, not only `Error` objects
Because the compiler cannot see which function in the try block threw
Because `strict` forbids `any` anywhere, including in catch clauses
Because `Error` is a DOM type that is missing from the Node typings
questions.why: You can throw a string, a number, anything, so `strict` (via `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, TS 4.4+) types it `unknown`. Narrow with `error instanceof Error` before reading `.message`, and keep a fallback. Knowing which call threw would not help: the thrown value is still arbitrary.
questions.asked: It checks whether you write catch blocks that survive a thrown string.

questions.q: What is `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>` for?
choices: Marking `loadUser` as async so that its callers are forced to await it
Waiting for `loadUser` to finish at runtime before checking its type
Getting the resolved data type of an async function without exporting it
Converting a callback-style `loadUser` into a promise-returning version
questions.why: `ReturnType` gives `Promise<User>`, and `Awaited` unwraps promises recursively, leaving `User`. It is purely type-level; nothing runs. Useful when a function's result type is inferred and never named.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can derive types from existing code instead of duplicating them.

questions.q: `tsc` passes and the API responses are validated, yet the app crashes on bad data. Which boundary is most often forgotten?
choices: Values read back from `localStorage`, env vars or `postMessage`
Function arguments passed between two modules of the same app
Props passed from a parent component to a typed child component
Return values of functions that have explicit return annotations
questions.why: The compiler checks everything it can see, which includes calls between your own typed modules and components. Data from storage, the environment or another window arrives as strings or `any` and is unchecked until you check it; stale `localStorage` from an older release is the classic crash.
questions.asked: A scenario question that tests whether you know every place untyped data enters, not just HTTP.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Extract<T, U>` and `Exclude<T, U>`?
choices: Extract works on object keys; Exclude works on union members
They are identical apart from the order of their two arguments
Extract pulls out one property type; Exclude removes a property
Extract keeps union members assignable to U; Exclude drops them
questions.why: Both are conditional types that distribute over a union. `Exclude<Status, 'archived'>` derives a narrower state set from a wider one without duplicating the list. Removing object properties is `Omit`'s job.
questions.asked: It checks that you can derive types from one source of truth instead of copying unions.

questions.q: Which single tsconfig setting most improves type safety in a new project?
choices: `"noEmit": true`
`"strict": true`
`"target": "ES2022"`
`"allowJs": true`
questions.why: `strict` is an umbrella over `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes` and more. `noEmit` and `target` change output, not checking; `allowJs` lets unchecked files in. Add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` once the team is comfortable.
questions.asked: 'What's in your tsconfig?' is a quick way to gauge experience.

questions.q: What return type does TypeScript give `lineTotal`?
choices: `any`, because the return type was never annotated
`number`, inferred from what the function returns
`unknown`, until a return annotation is added
`number | undefined`, as `total` may be unset
questions.why: Return types are inferred from the `return` expressions, and `number * number` is `number`. Parameters are what need annotations. Many teams still annotate exported functions' return types so a body change cannot silently change the public contract.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know where annotations earn their keep and where inference already covers you.

questions.q: Under `strict`, why does `function greet(name) { return 'Hi ' + name; }` fail to compile?
choices: Under `strict` every function must declare its return type as well
Untyped parameters default to `unknown`, and `+` rejects `unknown`
Function declarations need a type parameter list when arguments are untyped
`name` has no type and nothing to infer one from, so it is implicitly `any`
questions.why: `noImplicitAny`, part of `strict`, rejects a parameter that would silently become `any`. Return types can still be inferred, and parameters do not default to `unknown`. The fix is `name: string`; callbacks passed inline usually get their parameter types from context instead.
questions.asked: The first error every JavaScript developer hits when a project turns on `strict`.

questions.q: What is the type of `count`?
questions.code:
const entry: [string, number] = ['apples', 3];
const [label, count] = entry;
choices: number
string | number
any
number | undefined
questions.why: A tuple type fixes the type at each position, so destructuring position 1 gives `number`. `string | number` is what you would get from a plain `(string | number)[]` array, which is what the literal infers without the annotation.
questions.asked: Tuples are how hooks like `useState` return pairs, so this checks you can read their types.

questions.q: What lets `p.number` compile on the last line?
choices: Reading a key on a union is allowed if at least one member has that key
`in` is a runtime check only, so the compiler stops checking later lines
The `in` check narrowed `p`, so after the early return only `Card` is left
The inferred return type is `string`, which forces both branches to agree
questions.why: `'iban' in p` narrows `p` to `Bank` inside the `if`, and the early return leaves only `Card` afterwards. Without narrowing, `p.number` would fail, because on a union you can only read keys every member has.
questions.asked: Narrowing on a key is how you handle unions that have no shared tag field, common with third-party payloads.

questions.q: Why does this fail under `strict`?
choices: `Object.keys` accepts only `Record<string, unknown>`, not `object`
`typeof x === 'object'` narrows to `object`, but `object` is not iterable
The two returns have different types, so the return type cannot be inferred
`typeof null` is `'object'`, so `x` is still `object | null` there
questions.why: The compiler models the JavaScript quirk: `typeof null === 'object'`, so the branch narrows to `object | null` and the `Object.keys(x)` call rejects the possible `null`. Check `x !== null` as well, or use `x && typeof x === 'object'`.
questions.asked: It links a classic JavaScript quirk to the compiler error it causes, which is what real debugging looks like.

questions.q: What is `User`?
choices: { name: string; createdAt: string }
(name: string) => { name: string }
{ name: string; createdAt: Date }
typeof makeUser
questions.why: `typeof makeUser` gives the function's type, and `ReturnType` extracts what it returns, so the object type is derived from the code instead of written twice. `createdAt` is `Date` here; it only becomes a string after a JSON round trip, which the type does not know about.
questions.asked: Deriving types from code keeps one source of truth, which reviewers value over hand-copied interfaces.

questions.q: With `type Person = { name: string; id: number }`, how do `const a: Person = { name: 'Al' }` and `const b = { name: 'Al' } as Person` differ?
choices: They both compile, and each object gets an `id` of `0` at runtime
`a` fails because `id` is missing; `b` compiles, since `as` checks far less
`a` compiles and `b` fails, because `as` requires every property to exist
`as` converts the object at runtime; the annotation checks at compile time
questions.why: An annotation checks the literal fully, so the missing `id` is an error. `as` only requires the types to overlap, so it accepts an incomplete object and `b.id` is `undefined` at runtime. Neither converts anything. Prefer annotations or `satisfies`.
questions.asked: Reviewers see `as` used to silence errors daily; this checks you know what it gives up.

questions.q: What is the type of `city`?
choices: string | undefined
string | null | undefined
string | null
{ city: string } | undefined
questions.why: Optional chaining short-circuits to `undefined` when `address` is missing, so the compiler adds `| undefined`. It never produces `null`, even when the value it stops at is `null`.
questions.asked: It checks that you read `?.` as changing the type, which explains the 'possibly undefined' errors that follow it.

questions.q: Why is `keys` typed `string[]` rather than `(keyof User)[]`?
choices: `Object.keys` is declared in the JavaScript lib without generics, so nothing can be inferred from `user`
It is `string[]` only because `User` is a type alias; an interface gives `(keyof User)[]` instead
`keyof User` is a union, and an array of a union is not a legal return type for a lib function
Structural typing lets `user` carry extra runtime keys, so `id` and `name` are not guaranteed to be all of them
questions.why: Any object with at least `id` and `name` is a `User`, so at runtime it may carry more keys than the type lists, and `(keyof User)[]` would be a lie. When you know the object is exactly a `User`, cast: `Object.keys(user) as (keyof User)[]`, or iterate a literal list of keys instead. Alias versus interface plays no part.
questions.asked: The 'string cannot be used to index type User' error that follows is one of the most googled TypeScript errors, and the reason is structural typing.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.4+, does this compile under `strict`?
choices: No: narrowing never survives into a callback, so `input` is back to `string | null`
Yes: `input` is never reassigned, so its narrowing is kept inside the arrow function
No: parameters lose narrowing in closures; only `const` locals keep it there
Yes, but only because `map` runs the callback synchronously before returning
questions.why: Since TS 5.4 the checker keeps narrowing inside closures created after the last assignment to a `let` or parameter. Before 5.4 this was an error, which is why older code copies the value into a `const` first. Whether the callback runs synchronously is not something the checker knows or uses.
questions.asked: Shows whether you know narrowing is flow-based and why older codebases are full of `const x = input` copies.

questions.q: What is the runtime bug in this function?
choices: It fails to compile, because `!qty` does not narrow a `number` union
`qty` is still `number | undefined` on the last line, so it may print 'undefined'
It is fine: `!qty` is true only for `undefined`, which is the intended case
A quantity of 0 is falsy, so it is reported as 'not set' instead of '0 items'
questions.why: Truthiness narrowing removes `undefined` but also sends `0` (and `NaN`) down the 'missing' branch. The types are happy either way; use `qty === undefined` when zero is a real value. The narrowing itself works, so the other two type-level answers are wrong.
questions.asked: A real bug that ships constantly with prices, counts and page numbers; interviewers want `=== undefined` or `== null`.

questions.q: You have `interface User { id: string }`. Why can you not write `if (value instanceof User)`?
choices: Interfaces are erased, so there is no runtime value for `instanceof` to test against
`instanceof` works only on classes marked `abstract`, and interfaces are not classes
It compiles but always returns false, because interfaces have no prototype chain
`instanceof` needs a type guard declared alongside the interface to be usable
questions.why: `instanceof` is a JavaScript operator that needs a constructor function at runtime. An interface exists only for the checker, so tsc reports that `User` only refers to a type. Check the shape with `in`, a type guard or a schema instead.
questions.asked: Tests whether you keep the type world and the runtime world apart.

questions.q: What are the types of `a` and `b` inside the `if`?
choices: `a` is `string | number` and `b` is `string | boolean`; `===` does not narrow
`a` is `string | number` and `b` is `string`
Each is `string`, because that is the only type they share
Each is `never`, because the two unions are different types
questions.why: Equality narrowing intersects the possibilities: if `a === b` is true, both must be the one type the unions have in common, `string`. `===` is a narrowing construct just like `typeof`, and the unions only need to overlap, not match.
questions.asked: Checks that you know narrowing is broader than `typeof` and `in`.

questions.q: What is the type of `list`?
choices: `(string | string[])[]`
`string[]`
`string | string[]`
`any[]`
questions.why: `Array.isArray` is declared as a type predicate, so the true branch has `string[]` and the false branch `string`, which is wrapped in an array. Both arms are `string[]`. The nested-array option would only appear without narrowing.
questions.asked: The 'accept one or many' pattern is everywhere in API options, and interviewers like to see it typed cleanly.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.5+, what is the type of `ids`?
questions.code:
const raw = [1, null, 2, null];
const ids = raw.filter((x) => x !== null);
choices: `(number | null)[]`, because `filter` never changes the element type
`number[] | null[]`, split by the branches of the comparison
`number[]`, because the callback is inferred as a type predicate
`unknown[]`, because the callback returns a plain boolean
questions.why: TS 5.5 infers `x is number` for simple arrow functions like `x => x !== null`, and `filter` has an overload that uses predicates. Before 5.5 you got `(number | null)[]` and had to write the predicate yourself.
questions.asked: A good check that you have kept up with recent releases and know why the old `(x): x is T` boilerplate existed.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.9, what is the type of `names`?
questions.code:
declare const raw: (string | null)[];
const names = raw.filter(Boolean);
choices: `string[]`, because `Boolean` is typed as a type predicate
`boolean[]`, because `Boolean` converts each element to true or false
`(string | null)[]`, because `Boolean` is not a type predicate
`string[]`, because inferred predicates cover `Boolean`
questions.why: The built-in `Boolean` function is declared as returning `boolean`, not `value is T`, so no predicate overload applies and the element type is unchanged. Inferred predicates only apply to function expressions you write, such as `(x) => x !== null`, not to the `Boolean` constructor.
questions.asked: `filter(Boolean)` is a common idiom; knowing why it does not narrow shows you read the lib types.

questions.q: What does the compiler verify about the body of this type guard?
choices: That every property of `User` is checked before returning true
That the body narrows `x` to `User` on every path returning true
Only that it returns a boolean; the `x is User` claim is trusted
That the guard is only ever called with values typed `unknown`
questions.why: A type predicate is a promise you make to the checker. Here any non-null object passes as `User`, so callers get a `User` that may have no `email`. Keep guards next to tests, or derive them from a schema so they cannot drift.
questions.asked: Type guards are where many 'type-safe' codebases quietly lie; strong candidates say so unprompted.

questions.q: Why does the last line fail to compile?
choices: Assertion functions must be declared with the `function` keyword, never as arrows
Assertion calls need the callee's name to carry an explicit type annotation
`asserts v is string` is valid only on class methods, not on functions
An assertion function must return `boolean` as well as throwing
questions.why: The checker must know a call is an assertion before it infers types, so it requires the name to have an explicit type (error 2775). Write `const assertString: (v: unknown) => asserts v is string = ...` or use a `function` declaration. Arrows are fine once annotated, so 'never as arrows' is too strong.
questions.asked: Anyone who has written assertion helpers has hit this error; it separates using the feature from reading about it.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.3+, what is the type of `x` inside the `case`?
choices: `unknown`, so `toUpperCase` is a compile error
`string`, because `switch (true)` narrows by each case
`any`, because `switch (true)` switches type checking off
`string | unknown`, which collapses back to `unknown`
questions.why: TS 5.3 added narrowing for `switch (true)`: each `case` condition narrows as if it were an `if`. Earlier versions left `x` as `unknown` and reported an error on the call.
questions.asked: Lets you show you follow release notes and know the idiom is now type-safe.

questions.q: Does `payload` narrow after checking the destructured `kind`?
choices: No: once destructured, the two variables are unrelated to the checker
Only if you also write `payload as number` inside the `if`
Yes: destructured discriminants still narrow their sibling properties
Only when `Action` is declared as an interface, not a type alias
questions.why: Since TS 4.6, when you destructure a discriminated union into non-reassigned bindings, checking the discriminant narrows the other bindings too. Reassigning either binding, or destructuring with `let` and mutating, breaks the link.
questions.asked: Reducers and event handlers often destructure; knowing this saves pointless casts.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` inside the `if`?
choices: `unknown`: the check was stored in a variable, so it no longer narrows
`boolean`, since `isText` is the value being checked
`any`, because narrowing through a variable is unsound
`string`: a `const` holding the check still narrows `x`
questions.why: Since TS 4.4 the checker follows aliased conditions: a `const` initialised with a narrowing expression narrows the original when you test it, as long as neither is reassigned. Before 4.4 you got `unknown` here.
questions.asked: Naming a condition improves readability; interviewers like hearing that it no longer costs you type safety.

questions.q: What does `if (value == null)` narrow away in the `else` branch?
choices: Only `null`; `undefined` needs its own `=== undefined` check
`null`, `undefined`, `0` and empty strings, as loose equality coerces
Only `undefined`, because `null == undefined` is false
`null` and `undefined` together, and nothing else
questions.why: Loose equality with `null` is true for exactly `null` and `undefined`, and TypeScript narrows accordingly. It does not match `0` or `''` — that is truthiness. It is the one widely accepted use of `==`.
questions.asked: Checks you know the one legitimate `==` and do not confuse it with truthiness.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile under `strict`?
choices: `has` does not narrow `get`, which still returns `{ amount: number } | undefined`
`Map` keys must be declared `readonly`, and `sku` is a mutable function parameter
`get` needs a generic argument when the value type is an object literal
`has` narrows `sku` to `never`, so the `get` call has no valid overload
questions.why: The checker has no link between two separate method calls, so `get` is always `V | undefined`. Call `get` once, store the result and check it: `const hit = cache.get(sku); if (hit) return hit.amount;`. That is also one lookup instead of two.
questions.asked: Everyone hits this; the good answer is 'get once and test the result', not a `!`.

questions.q: What is the type of `x.id` inside the `if` (TypeScript 4.9+)?
choices: `any`, because `in` narrows to an index signature
`string | number`, the possible property key types
`unknown`, because only the key's presence is known
A compile error: `in` cannot narrow an `object`
questions.why: Since TS 4.9, `'id' in x` narrows `object` to `object & Record<'id', unknown>`. You know the key exists but nothing about its value, so check `typeof x.id` next. `string | number` confuses the key type with the value type.
questions.asked: The building block of every hand-written guard for JSON; shows you can validate without casting.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` inside the `if`?
choices: `number`, as the `typeof` check says
`string`, since checks cannot contradict the parameter
`never`, since no `string` can pass the check
A compile error: the comparison has no overlap
questions.why: Narrowing a `string` by `typeof x === 'number'` leaves no possible type, so `x` is `never`. tsc does not report this comparison as an error because `typeof` returns the general union of type-name strings. Seeing `never` in a hover is a useful sign of dead code.
questions.asked: Recognising `never` in a hover as 'this branch is impossible' is a practical debugging skill.

questions.q: This compiles under `strict`. What happens when `use()` runs with `value` set?
choices: It returns 1, since the narrowing guarantees `value` is still a non-empty string
It throws a TypeError, as `clear()` set `value` to null after the check
It returns undefined, since reading `length` of null gives undefined
It returns 0, since `clear()` sets `value` to an empty string
questions.why: TypeScript deliberately does not reset property narrowing after function calls; doing so would make most code unusable. So `this.value` stays `string` in the checker's eyes, yet at runtime it is null and `.length` throws. Copy the value into a local `const` before calling anything that might mutate.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know the checker's trade-offs, not just its rules.

questions.q: What does this line do?
questions.code:
let id: string | number = 'abc';
id.toUpperCase();
choices: Fails: `id` is declared `string | number`, so `toUpperCase` is not allowed
Compiles: assignment narrows `id` to `string` until it is reassigned
Compiles, but only because `let` declarations are not type-checked
Fails: a union-typed variable must be narrowed with `typeof` first
questions.why: The declared type is `string | number`, but assignment narrowing gives the variable the assigned type for the code that follows. Assigning a number later narrows it to `number` from that point on.
questions.asked: Distinguishes the declared type from the flow type, which explains many confusing hovers.

questions.q: What is the type of `label` on the last line?
choices: `string | (() => string)`
`string`
`Function | string`
`unknown`
questions.why: `typeof l === 'function'` narrows to the function member, whose call returns `string`; the other branch is already `string`. This 'value or factory' shape is common in config and React props.
questions.asked: Accepting a value or a lazy factory is a common option-typing task.

questions.q: What makes `r.value` compile on the last line?
choices: The `return` in the `if` narrows `r` to the `ok: true` member afterwards
`value` is optional on every member, so reading it always compiles
The union is merged into one object type with all four properties
`!r.ok` is a type guard only because `ok` was declared as `boolean`
questions.why: `ok` is a literal `true`/`false` discriminant, so `!r.ok` narrows to the failure member, and the early return leaves only the success member below it. If `ok` were plain `boolean`, nothing would narrow.
questions.asked: The `ok: true | false` result shape is everywhere; this checks you know why the literal types matter.

questions.q: What is the type of `city` on the last line?
choices: `string | undefined`, because optional chaining never narrows
A compile error: `u.address` is possibly undefined
`string`, with `u.address` narrowed to defined as well
`string | null`, as `?.` converts undefined to null
questions.why: A truthy `u.address?.city` implies `u.address` is defined, and TypeScript narrows the whole chain. `?.` yields `undefined`, never `null`, when it short-circuits.
questions.asked: Quick check that you trust narrowing instead of sprinkling `!`.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.5+, does this compile under `strict`?
choices: No: element access with a plain `string` key is never narrowed by `typeof`
Yes: `obj[key]` narrows because neither `obj` nor `key` is reassigned
No: `Record` values must be read with `Object.entries` to narrow
Yes, but only because `Record` values are implicitly `any`
questions.why: TS 5.5 narrows element accesses when both the object and the key are effectively constant. Earlier versions required `const v = obj[key]` first. Values of a `Record<string, V>` are typed `V`, not `any`.
questions.asked: Shows you know which narrowing limitations recent releases removed, and why the local-variable workaround existed.

questions.q: Why does this narrowing fail under `strict`?
choices: `kind` is typed `string`, so the check cannot narrow and `radius` stays optional
`Math.PI` is a `number` literal, which cannot be multiplied by an optional
The `**` operator is rejected on any property that is declared optional
Comparing a `string` to the literal `'circle'` is itself a type error under `strict`
questions.why: Narrowing needs a union with literal discriminants. With one object type and a `string` kind, nothing ties `kind === 'circle'` to `radius` being set. Model it as `{ kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number }`.
questions.asked: The 'bag of optionals' is the most common modelling mistake; the fix is the discriminated union.

questions.q: What is the type of `n` on the last line?
choices: `any`, because `n` was declared without a type or initialiser
`number`, because `null` is dropped from inferred variable types
`number | null`, from control-flow analysis of the assignments
`unknown`, because the checker cannot follow both branches
questions.why: A `let` with no annotation and no initialiser is an 'evolving' variable under `noImplicitAny`: its type is computed from the assignments that reach each use. Both branches reach the return, giving `number | null`. It only becomes an implicit-any error if the checker cannot determine a type.
questions.asked: Explains a confusing hover and shows you understand flow-based typing rather than memorised rules.

questions.q: Why does the last line fail to compile under `strict`?
choices: `find` returns `User | undefined`, because nothing may match
`find` returns `User[]`, so `.name` needs an index first
`find` returns `unknown` unless you pass a type argument
The callback must be a type predicate for `find` to compile
questions.why: `Array.prototype.find` is typed `T | undefined` because a search can come up empty, and `strictNullChecks` makes you handle that. A predicate callback only narrows the element type; it does not remove `undefined`. Decide what 'not found' means (404, default, throw) instead of adding `!`.
questions.asked: Every CRUD handler looks something up; the interviewer wants to hear what you do when it is not there.

questions.q: Under `strict`, what does tsc report for this class?
choices: Nothing: `connect` assigns `db` before it can be used
An error: `db` is private, so a method like `connect` cannot assign it
An error: `db` has no initialiser and is not set in the constructor
Nothing: class fields are only checked when they are read through `this`
questions.why: `strictPropertyInitialization` requires every non-optional field to be assigned in its declaration or the constructor; a later method call does not count. Pass `db` to the constructor, make the field `Db | undefined`, or, if something outside guarantees it, use `db!: Db`.
questions.asked: Shows whether you model 'not ready yet' honestly or paper over it with `!`.

questions.q: What does the `!` in `private db!: Db` tell the compiler?
choices: That `db` is set before use by something it cannot see
That `db` must never be assigned `null` at runtime
That `db` is set once and then becomes read-only
That reads of `db` get a runtime null check inserted
questions.why: The definite-assignment assertion switches off the initialisation check for that field, typically for frameworks that inject values after construction. Nothing is emitted, so if the promise is wrong you get `undefined` at runtime. It says nothing about later assignments or immutability.
questions.asked: Common in ORM entities and Angular code; strong candidates explain that it moves the risk rather than removing it.

questions.q: What are the types of `a` and `b`?
questions.code:
let a = 'dark';
const b = 'dark';
choices: `string` and `string`
`'dark'` and `'dark'`
`'dark'` and `string`
`string` and `'dark'`
questions.why: A `let` can be reassigned, so its literal type is widened to `string`. A `const` primitive can never change, so it keeps the literal type `'dark'`. This is why passing a `let` to a parameter typed `'dark' | 'light'` fails.
questions.asked: The foundation for understanding every 'string is not assignable to ...' error.

questions.q: Why does the last call fail, and what is the cleanest fix?
choices: `method` widened to `string`; annotate `opts` or add `as const` to it
`url` is not a `Method`; move `method` to be the first property instead
`opts` has an extra property; spread it into a new object in the call
Literal unions cannot be passed via a variable; inline the object literal
questions.why: A mutable object's properties are widened, so `method` is `string`. Annotating (`const opts: SendOptions = ...`) or `as const` keeps the literal. Inlining also works because it is contextually typed, but it is a workaround, not the rule the other options state.
questions.asked: Extremely common with fetch options and config objects; the follow-up is usually 'annotate or satisfies?'.

questions.q: What does TypeScript infer as the return type of `level`?
choices: `string`, as return values are always widened
`string | undefined`, for the fall-through
`'high'`, the first return statement wins
`'high' | 'low'`
questions.why: Literal return values are collected into a union of literal types, so callers can compare against exactly `'high'` or `'low'`. The value only widens to `string` when assigned to a mutable location. Every path returns, so there is no `undefined`.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know when inference keeps literals, which decides if a switch over the result is exhaustive.

questions.q: What is the type of `row`?
questions.code: const row = [42, 'Ann'];
choices: `[number, string]`, a tuple
`(string | number)[]`
`readonly [42, 'Ann']`, a literal tuple
`any[]`, due to the mixed types
questions.why: Array literals are inferred as arrays of the union of their element types, not as tuples, because arrays are usually grown and iterated. Add a tuple annotation for `[number, string]`, or `as const` for the readonly literal tuple.
questions.asked: Explains why functions returning pairs need an annotation, which leads to the tuple follow-ups.

questions.q: What is `Role` here?
questions.code:
const ROLE = { Admin: 'admin', Editor: 'editor' } as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLE)[keyof typeof ROLE];
choices: `'Admin' | 'Editor'`, the keys
`string`, since values widen
`'admin' | 'editor'`
`typeof ROLE`, the object type
questions.why: `keyof typeof ROLE` is the keys, and indexing with them gives the value types, which `as const` kept as literals. This 'enum-like object' gives you a runtime object to iterate plus a union type, with no `enum` emit. Without `as const` it would be `string`.
questions.asked: The standard enum alternative in modern codebases; you should be able to write it from memory.

questions.q: In this handler, why is `e.key` typed with no annotation on `e`?
choices: Implicit `any` is allowed for callback parameters, even under the `strict` flag
The DOM library marks every event handler parameter as `any`
Contextual typing: the `'keydown'` overload fixes `e` as `KeyboardEvent`
TypeScript infers `e` from how the body uses it, i.e. from `e.key`
questions.why: The callback's parameter type comes from where the function is passed: `addEventListener` maps `'keydown'` to `KeyboardEvent`. TypeScript never infers parameter types from how the body uses them. Move the arrow into a separate `const` and the context is lost, giving an implicit-`any` error.
questions.asked: Contextual typing explains when annotations are needed and when they are noise.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.2+, what does this do?
questions.code:
declare const ids: string[] | number[];
const doubled = ids.map((x) => x);
choices: Fails: the two `map` signatures of the union cannot be called together
Fails: you must narrow with `Array.isArray` before calling any array method
Compiles: `x` is `any`, because the union of signatures is ambiguous
Compiles: `x` is `string | number` and `doubled` is `(string | number)[]`
questions.why: Since TS 5.2, calling methods like `map`, `filter` and `find` on a union of array types treats it as an array of the element union. Older versions reported that the union's signatures were not compatible. `Array.isArray` would not help anyway: both members are arrays.
questions.asked: Probes whether you understand calling methods on unions and have kept up with the fix.

questions.q: What is the type of `id`?
choices: `string | number`, a union of both
`string`, as the first type wins
`never`
A compile error on the `A & B` type
questions.why: An intersection requires both: `id` must be a `string` and a `number` at once, which is `never`. TypeScript does not report the conflict when you write `A & B`. `interface B extends A` would report the incompatibility, which is one reason to prefer `extends` for object shapes.
questions.asked: Explains a silent failure mode of intersections and the practical case for `extends`.

questions.q: `type Status = 'draft' | 'live' | 'archived'`. Which approach makes adding a fourth status a compile error at every place that labels statuses?
choices: `const labels: Partial<Record<Status, string>>`, so missing keys are flagged
`const labels = new Map<Status, string>()`, with one `set` call per status
`const labels: Record<Status, string>` with one entry per status
`const labels: { [key: string]: string }` with the three current keys
questions.why: `Record<Status, string>` requires a key for every member, so a new status is flagged until you add its label. `Partial` makes every key optional, a `Map` is never checked for completeness, and a string index signature accepts any keys at all.
questions.asked: A lookup table is often cleaner than a switch; interviewers like hearing that it can be exhaustive too.

questions.q: Why does this call fail under `strict`?
choices: `reduce` is not one of the methods that exist on `readonly number[]`
Readonly arrays can only be passed to generic functions
`readonly` arrays cannot hold numeric literals like `1`
`total` could mutate the array, so a readonly one is refused
questions.why: `number[]` has `push`, `sort` and friends; `readonly number[]` does not, so it is not assignable to the mutable type. If `total` does not mutate, type its parameter `readonly number[]`: it then accepts both. Non-mutating methods like `reduce` exist on readonly arrays.
questions.asked: Leads into 'type parameters by what the function needs', a sign of good API design.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.0+, which line fails to compile?
choices: Neither `b` nor `c`: numeric enums accept any number
Only `c`, because 5 is not a value of any `Dir` member
`b` and `c`, because raw numbers need `Dir.` access
Only `a`, because `Dir.Up` has the value 0, which is falsy
questions.why: TS 5.0 made all enums union enums: a numeric literal is assignable only if it matches a member's value. `1` is `Dir.Down`, so `b` compiles; `5` does not. Older versions accepted any number, which made numeric enums leaky.
questions.asked: Checks whether your enum knowledge is current; many people still repeat the pre-5.0 'any number' rule.

questions.q: Why does the assignment fail?
questions.code:
enum Status { Active = 'active', Closed = 'closed' }
const s: Status = 'active';
choices: String enum members must be written in upper case to be assignable
The value must come from `Status.Active`, not a string literal
`const` cannot hold a string enum value; use a `let` declaration instead
Enums need `as const` before their members can be used
questions.why: String enums are nominal in this direction: a matching string literal is not assignable to the enum type. That is why values parsed from JSON need a cast or a mapping to become `Status`, and a key reason teams prefer `'active' | 'closed'` unions for API fields.
questions.asked: The practical cost of enums at API boundaries; a strong answer ties it to parsing JSON.

questions.q: What does a regular (non-`const`) `enum Color { Red, Green }` compile to?
choices: Nothing: like interfaces and type aliases, enums are erased completely
A frozen array `['Red', 'Green']` that is indexed by position
A union of the numbers 0 and 1, with no runtime representation of names
A runtime object mapping names to values and numbers back to names
questions.why: Enums are one of the few TypeScript features that emit JavaScript: an object with `Red: 0` and, for numeric enums, a reverse mapping `0: 'Red'`. That emitted code is why Node's type stripping and `erasableSyntaxOnly` reject enums.
questions.asked: Knowing what emits code is increasingly relevant now that Node runs TypeScript by stripping types.

questions.q: Why can `(n) => n * 2` be passed where `(value: number, index: number, array: number[]) => number` is expected?
choices: Extra parameters are filled in by an implicit `any` rest parameter
It cannot: the callback must declare all three parameters to match
A function taking fewer parameters can safely ignore extra arguments
Parameter counts are only compared when `strictFunctionTypes` is switched off
questions.why: Calling a function with extra arguments is harmless in JavaScript, so TypeScript lets a shorter parameter list satisfy a longer one. The reverse, a callback that requires more parameters than will be passed, is an error. `strictFunctionTypes` affects parameter types, not counts.
questions.asked: Explains why every `map` callback compiles, and tests how you reason about assignability.

questions.q: Why does this signature end with `= {}`?
choices: It sets the return type of `list` to an object literal
It makes `page` and `size` required inside the body
It is required for destructuring to type-check at all
It lets callers write `list()` with no argument at all
questions.why: Without the default, calling `list()` would destructure `undefined` and throw, and the parameter would be required. The inner defaults make `page` and `size` plain `number` in the body; the outer `= {}` makes the whole argument optional.
questions.asked: The options-object pattern is standard for API functions; this checks you can type it correctly.

questions.q: What is the type of `setName` when you destructure the result of `useField()`?
choices: `(next: string) => void`, the setter itself
`string | ((next: string) => void)`
`[string, (next: string) => void]`
`unknown`, because array returns are not inferred
questions.why: The returned array literal is inferred as `(string | ((next: string) => void))[]`, so each destructured element is the whole union and neither is usable without narrowing. Add `as const` to the return or annotate the return type as a tuple.
questions.asked: Anyone who has written a hook-style helper has hit this; the fix shows you understand tuple inference.

questions.q: What do labels like `start` and `end` add in `type Range = [start: number, end: number]`?
choices: Documentation in hovers and signatures; the type is still a pair
Runtime property names, so `range.start` works on the value
They let the tuple be destructured by name as an object
A requirement to pass the two values as an object literal `{ start, end }`
questions.why: Tuple labels are purely for readability: editors show them in hovers, and they appear in rest-parameter signatures. The value is still an array indexed by position, so `range.start` does not exist.
questions.asked: Quick check on reading types; a strong answer mentions they document rest-parameter signatures.

questions.q: `input` is a `string`. Why does `input as number` fail to compile?
choices: `as` only works on values typed `any` or `unknown`
`as` cannot be used on primitive types, only objects
Neither type is assignable to the other, so tsc refuses
`as` would need a runtime conversion, which tsc never emits
questions.why: An assertion is allowed only when one type is assignable to the other; `string` and `number` do not overlap, so tsc says to go through `unknown` first. That double cast silences the error but converts nothing: use `Number(input)` for a real conversion.
questions.asked: Separates people who think `as` converts values from people who know it only changes the compiler's view.

questions.q: What does tsc report for `B`?
questions.code:
interface A { id: string }
interface B extends A { id: number }
choices: Nothing: `B`'s `id` overrides `A`'s, as in a class
Nothing, but `id` becomes `never` on `B`
An error: `B` incorrectly extends `A`
Nothing: `id` on `B` becomes `string | number`
questions.why: `extends` checks that the new interface is assignable to the base, so an incompatible property type is reported where you wrote it. The intersection `A & { id: number }` silently produces `id: never` instead, which is why `extends` gives better errors.
questions.asked: Pairs with the intersection question; interviewers like the 'better error messages' reasoning.

questions.q: What is the difference between `private secret` and `#secret` on a class?
choices: `private` is compile-time only; `#secret` is enforced by JavaScript at runtime
`#secret` is compile-time only; `private` is enforced by the JavaScript engine
`private` fields are shared by instances; `#` fields are per-instance only
`#secret` may be read by subclasses, while `private` hides it from them too
questions.why: TypeScript's `private` disappears when compiled, so `(obj as any).secret` or plain JavaScript can still read it. `#secret` is a JavaScript private field: inaccessible outside the class body at runtime, including to subclasses. Neither is shared between instances.
questions.asked: Checks you know which guarantees come from TypeScript and which from JavaScript.

questions.q: Under `strict`, what does tsc report for this class?
choices: Nothing: `msg` is inferred as `string` from the interface
An error: `msg` implicitly has an `any` type
Nothing: `implements` switches off implicit-any checks
An error: `Log` must use `extends`, not `implements`
questions.why: `implements` only checks the finished class against the interface; it does not contextually type the class's members. So `msg` has no type and `noImplicitAny` reports it. Annotate the parameter yourself.
questions.asked: A surprise for most people; knowing it shows you understand what `implements` does and does not do.

questions.q: Why does this type fail to compile?
choices: `name` is a string key, so its type must fit the `number` index signature
An index signature must be the last member written in the type literal
Index signatures are only allowed in interfaces, not type aliases
The `player` placeholder must be written as `key` in an index signature
questions.why: A string index signature says every string key maps to `number`, and `name` is a string key, so it must be a `number` too. Split the data: `{ name: string; scores: Record<string, number> }`. Member order and the placeholder name do not matter.
questions.asked: Shows whether you can model a dictionary alongside fixed fields without reaching for `any`.

questions.q: What is the type of `k`?
choices: `string`, the index signature key type
`string | number`
`never`, as there are no named keys
`'key'`, the placeholder name
questions.why: JavaScript converts numeric property keys to strings, so a string index signature also accepts number keys and `keyof` reports `string | number`. That is why `keyof T` is often wrapped as `Extract<keyof T, string>` or `string & keyof T` in generic code.
questions.asked: Explains the `string & keyof T` idiom you see in library code.

questions.q: Which line fails to compile?
choices: Line A, because `message` is not on every member
Line B, because `!== 'idle'` cannot narrow a union type
Line C, because only `idle` remains and it has no `data`
No line: `data` is treated as optional on the idle member
questions.why: After the first check removes `error`, `!== 'idle'` leaves only `ok`, so line B is fine. What reaches line C is `{ status: 'idle' }`, which has no `data`. Negative checks narrow just like positive ones.
questions.asked: The loading/ok/error union is the most common app-state type; reading narrowing through several checks is basic fluency.

questions.q: A cached state `{ status: 'done'; at: Date }` is saved with `JSON.stringify` and read back with `JSON.parse(...) as State`. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing: `JSON.parse` revives `Date` objects when the type says `Date`
`status` comes back as a plain `string`, so the union no longer narrows
`at` comes back as an ISO string, but the type still claims it is a `Date`
`JSON.stringify` throws on `Date` values unless a replacer function is given
questions.why: `Date` serialises to an ISO string and `JSON.parse` does not know your types, so `state.at.getTime()` throws although it type-checks. `status` survives as the same string, which still narrows at runtime; only the cast is the lie. Parse and convert on the way in.
questions.asked: A classic localStorage and API bug; interviewers want to hear 'the cast lies, parse on the way in'.

questions.q: Why does `x.a` fail to compile?
choices: Discriminants must be `string`, and `kind` is an object literal type
The discriminant is nested, so checking it narrows `x.meta`, not `x`
`meta` needs to be marked `readonly` before its fields can narrow
`===` narrows only when the literal is written on the left side
questions.why: A discriminant must be a property of the union members themselves; a literal-typed field one level down does not narrow the parent. Lift `kind` to the top level. Neither `readonly` nor operand order affects narrowing.
questions.asked: Comes up when API payloads nest their type tag; knowing the limit tells you when to reshape the data.

questions.q: Why does the call fail to compile?
choices: A union of functions cannot be called until it is narrowed with `typeof`
The call resolves to the first member, so `x` must be a `string & number`
`'a'` must be wrapped as `String('a')` to match the first signature
The argument must satisfy every member, so its type is `string & number`
questions.why: Calling a union of functions is only safe with an argument every member accepts, so parameters are intersected: `string & number`, which is `never`. Unions of functions are callable, just rarely usefully. Model it as one function taking `string | number`.
questions.asked: Shows you can reason about why an error mentions `never`, instead of guessing at casts.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.1+, which function compiles under `strict`?
choices: Only `b`, because a missing return means `void`
`a` and `b`, but not `c`
All three, since each return type allows `undefined`
`b` and `c`, because `undefined` needs a `return`
questions.why: Since TS 5.1 a function whose declared return type is `undefined` may omit `return` entirely, just like `void`. A union such as `string | undefined` still needs an explicit return on every path, so `c` is error 2355.
questions.asked: Probes whether your mental model of `void` versus `undefined` is current.

questions.q: What is the type of `id` on the last line?
choices: `string | undefined`, because `fail` may return
`string | never`, which stays as written in hovers
`string`, because a `never` operand adds nothing
`unknown`, because the two operands' types differ
questions.why: `never` means the call does not complete, so it contributes nothing to the union: `string | never` is `string`. This makes a throwing helper a neat way to enforce required values inline. The `never` annotation is what tells tsc that `fail` cannot return.
questions.asked: A practical `never` use; interviewers like it more than the textbook definition.

questions.q: `onChange?: (value: string) => void` is an optional prop. What is the idiomatic way to call it?
choices: `onChange?.(value)`, which calls it only if it is defined
`onChange!(value)`, because the parent always passes it
`onChange(value)`, as optional functions become no-ops
`(onChange as Function)(value)`, to satisfy the checker
questions.why: Optional call syntax short-circuits to `undefined` when the function is missing. `!` asserts it exists and crashes when it does not, and nothing turns a missing function into a no-op for you.
questions.asked: Quick fluency check with optional callbacks, common in component and event APIs.

questions.q: What is `Options`?
questions.code:
const defaults = { retries: 3, timeoutMs: 5000, verbose: false };
type Options = typeof defaults;
choices: `{ retries: 3; timeoutMs: 5000; verbose: false }`
`{ retries: number; timeoutMs: number; verbose: boolean }`
`'object'`, the string that `typeof` returns at runtime
`{ retries?: number; timeoutMs?: number; verbose?: boolean }`
questions.why: In a type position, `typeof` asks for the declared type of a value, and the object's properties were widened because they are mutable. The runtime `typeof` operator is a different thing. Nothing becomes optional unless you wrap it in `Partial`.
questions.asked: Deriving types from values keeps one source of truth; interviewers look for it.

questions.q: How do you type a function that also carries a property, like `fetcher` with a `fetcher.retries` number?
choices: `type Fetcher = { (url: string): Promise<Response>; retries: number }`
`type Fetcher = ((url: string) => Promise<Response>) | { retries: number }`
`interface Fetcher extends Function { retries: number; url: string }`
It cannot be typed, because functions cannot have properties in TypeScript
questions.why: An object type with a call signature describes something callable that also has properties. The union means 'either a function or an object', and extending `Function` loses the parameter types. TypeScript also recognises property assignments on function declarations (`fetcher.retries = 3`).
questions.asked: Call signatures show up in library types; being able to write one shows you can read them.

questions.q: Why do many codebases wrap `JSON.parse` in a helper that returns `unknown`?
choices: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, which silently disables checking on everything that follows
`JSON.parse` returns `object`, which is too narrow for arrays, numbers and plain strings
`JSON.parse` returns `string`, which must be cast before any property is accessible
`JSON.parse` is untyped in lib.dom, so every call to it is an implicit-any error
questions.why: The lib declares `JSON.parse(text): any`, so the result flows anywhere without a check. Returning `unknown` forces callers to validate or narrow before use. The other options misstate its declared return type.
questions.asked: Shows you know where `any` enters a codebase without anyone typing it.

questions.q: What does `(string & {})` achieve in this type?
choices: It rejects `'42px'`, so only the three preset sizes are allowed
It accepts any string but keeps the presets in autocomplete
It turns `Size` into a branded, nominal string type
It forces custom strings through a type assertion
questions.why: Plain `'sm' | ... | string` collapses to `string`, and editors lose the suggestions. `string & {}` is still every string but is not reduced, so the literals survive for autocomplete while arbitrary strings are accepted.
questions.asked: A common pattern in design-system and library props; recognising it shows you read real-world types.

questions.q: Why does the last line fail, and what is a clean fix?
choices: `includes` needs a readonly argument; pass `input as const`
`as const` arrays have no `includes`; convert with `Array.from`
`includes` takes a `Size`; write a guard `isSize(x): x is Size`
`input` is `string`, so compare with `SIZES.indexOf(input) > 0`
questions.why: On `readonly ('sm'|'md'|'lg')[]`, `includes` expects the element type, so an arbitrary `string` is rejected. Wrap it in a guard: `(SIZES as readonly string[]).includes(x)` inside `isSize(x: string): x is Size`, which also narrows `input` for the caller. `indexOf` has the same parameter type.
questions.asked: Validating a string against an allowed list is daily work; interviewers want the guard, not a scattered cast.

questions.q: What are the types of `a` and `b`?
questions.code:
const a = document.querySelector('input');
const b = document.querySelector('#email');
choices: `HTMLInputElement | null` and `HTMLInputElement | null`
`HTMLInputElement` and `Element`, as both are found
`Element | null` and `Element | null`
`HTMLInputElement | null` and `Element | null`
questions.why: `querySelector` has an overload keyed on tag names, so `'input'` maps to `HTMLInputElement`. An id selector could match anything, so it returns `Element`. Both may find nothing, hence `| null`.
questions.asked: Everyday DOM typing; the follow-up is usually how to get an input from `'#email'` safely.

questions.q: What does the type argument in `document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#email')` check?
choices: It checks the matched element's tag name at runtime before returning it
It returns `null` whenever the match is not an `<input>` element
It fails to compile unless the selector string starts with `input`
Nothing: it is an unchecked cast of the result to that element type
questions.why: The generic overload just lets you pick the return type, so it is a cast written differently. If `#email` is a `<div>`, `.value` is `undefined`. For a checked version, test `el instanceof HTMLInputElement`.
questions.asked: Many people think generic arguments are checks; this separates them from those who know they are casts.

questions.q: Why prefer `satisfies` over an annotation here?
choices: With the annotation, `routes.hme` compiles as `string`; here it is caught
`satisfies` also checks at runtime that each value is a route that exists
The annotation would turn `home` and `about` into optional properties
`satisfies` is the only form that allows `routes` to be exported
questions.why: Annotating as `Record<string, string>` makes every string key valid, so a typo compiles and returns `undefined`. `satisfies` checks the shape but keeps the inferred type with its exact keys, so `hme` is an error. Nothing is checked at runtime either way.
questions.asked: The canonical argument for `satisfies`; a strong answer names the lost-keys problem specifically.

questions.q: What does `as const satisfies Record<string, `/${string}`>` give you on a routes object?
choices: Readonly literal values that are also checked against the constraint
A type widened to the constraint, then made readonly at every level down
A runtime freeze plus a runtime check of each path's leading slash
Literal values that may be reassigned later, as long as they fit
