questions.why: `as const` keeps each value as a readonly literal like `'/about'`; `satisfies` then checks those values fit the template-literal constraint without widening them. Neither does anything at runtime: `as const` does not call `Object.freeze`.
questions.asked: A modern config idiom; explaining both halves shows you understand what each operator contributes.

questions.q: What is `K`?
choices: `'id' | 'name' | 'total'`
`'name' | 'total'`
`never`
questions.why: A value of type `A | B` is only guaranteed to have the keys both members share, so `keyof` of a union is the intersection of the key sets. `keyof (A & B)` would give all three. This is why you cannot read `name` without narrowing first.
questions.asked: Tests whether you reason about unions as 'one of these values' rather than 'all these fields'.

questions.q: What is the type of `result`?
choices: `({ id: number } | string[])[]`
`[{ id: number }, string[]]`
`Promise<[{ id: number }, string[]]>`
`unknown[]`
questions.why: `Promise.all` is typed with a mapped tuple, so an array literal of promises gives a tuple of their resolved values, in order. `await` unwraps the outer promise. That is what makes `const [user, tags] = await Promise.all(...)` fully typed.
questions.asked: Parallel fetching is daily work, and interviewers like candidates who know the destructured result stays typed.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
choices: Nothing: `async` functions return their value directly
An error: `async` functions must declare a return type
Nothing: tsc inserts the missing `await` for you when compiling
An error: `Promise<number>` is not assignable to `number`
questions.why: An `async` function always returns a promise, so its inferred return type is `Promise<number>`. You need `await total()` inside an async context. Return type annotations are optional, though `Promise<number>` would be the correct one.
questions.asked: Basic, but it catches people who treat `async` as decoration.

questions.q: `isAdmin(user)` returns `Promise<boolean>`. What does tsc report for `if (isAdmin(user)) { ... }`?
choices: Nothing: a promise is always truthy, so the condition is valid code
Nothing, but the `if` body waits for the promise to settle before it runs
Nothing, but the `if` body waits for the promise to settle first
An error: the condition is always true because the promise is defined
questions.why: TS reports error 2801 when a promise is used directly as a condition, since a promise object is always truthy. It catches the missing `await` that would otherwise grant admin to everyone. `if` does not generally require `boolean`; this check is specific to promises.
questions.asked: A security-shaped bug; knowing tsc catches it, and when it cannot, shows real experience.

questions.q: This compiles. Why is it still a bug?
choices: `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so `saveAll` resolves at once
`forEach` runs the callbacks one at a time and ignores the `await`
`forEach` rejects async callbacks at runtime by throwing a TypeError
`await` inside a callback blocks the whole event loop until done
questions.why: `forEach` expects a callback returning `void`, and a function returning a promise is assignable to that, so tsc is silent. The promises are dropped: `saveAll` resolves before saving finishes and rejections go unhandled. Use `for...of` with `await` or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))`.
questions.asked: One of the most common async bugs; the lint rule `no-misused-promises` exists because tsc allows it.

questions.q: In a `.ts` file with no `import` or `export`, why does `const name = 'Ann';` fail to compile?
choices: `name` is a reserved word in TypeScript, so it cannot be a variable name
String literals cannot be assigned to a `const` in a global scope
Top-level `const` declarations are only allowed inside ES module files
The file is a global script, so it clashes with the DOM's global `name`
questions.why: A file without top-level `import`/`export` is a script, and its declarations share the global scope with lib.dom, which declares `window.name`. Adding `export {}` (or any import) makes it a module with its own scope; `moduleDetection: force` does the same project-wide.
questions.asked: Baffling the first time; the fix shows you understand scripts versus modules.

questions.q: What does this line declare?
questions.code:
declare const user: { id: number; name: string };
const { id: number } = user;
choices: A variable `id` with the type `number`
A variable named `number` holding `user.id`
A compile error, as `number` is a reserved type
A variable `id` checked to be a number at runtime
questions.why: In destructuring, `key: name` renames, so this creates a variable called `number`. Types go after the whole pattern: `const { id }: { id: number } = user`. It compiles, which is what makes it a trap.
questions.asked: A classic stumble when typing destructured parameters; spotting it is a quick fluency check.

questions.q: What is the difference between `string[]` and `Array<string>`?
choices: `Array<string>` is a class instance; `string[]` is a plain object
`string[]` is fixed-length; `Array<string>` can grow and shrink
None: they are two spellings of the same type
`Array<string>` allows holes; `string[]` requires dense arrays
questions.why: `T[]` is shorthand for `Array<T>`, and `readonly T[]` is shorthand for `ReadonlyArray<T>`. Style guides pick one for consistency; the generic form can read better for complex element types like `Array<string | number>`.
questions.asked: A warm-up question; the good answer adds the readonly equivalent.

questions.q: A `User` type comes from the API. The UI adds `isSelected`. Which is the better model?
choices: Add `isSelected?: boolean` to `User` so both layers share one type
Keep `User` as is and track selection as a `Set<User['id']>` alongside
Cast API responses with `as User & { isSelected: boolean }` on arrival
Create a class `SelectableUser extends User` and convert every item
questions.why: Selection is UI state, not part of the entity, so keeping a set of ids avoids polluting the API type and avoids copying every item to toggle one. An optional field blurs the contract for every other consumer, and the cast claims a property that is not there.
questions.asked: Separating server data from UI state is a recurring design question in CRUD interviews.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this signature?
choices: Nothing; callers may simply pass `undefined` for `query`
An error: a required parameter cannot follow an optional one
Nothing; `limit` becomes optional because it follows `query`
An error only at call sites that leave out the `query` argument
questions.why: Optional parameters must come after all required ones, because positional arguments cannot skip a slot. Either move `limit` first, give `query` a default, or type it `string | undefined` so callers pass `undefined` explicitly.
questions.asked: It checks you know how optional parameters map to positional arguments, a common source of awkward APIs.

questions.q: How do callers see the parameter `name` in this function?
choices: As a required `string`, since the default only applies inside
As the literal type `'friend'`, inferred from the default
As `name?: string`, so it can be omitted or passed `undefined`
As `any`, since the parameter has no explicit type annotation
questions.why: A default value makes the parameter optional to callers and gives it the widened type of the default, here `string`. Passing `undefined` also triggers the default; the literal type is widened just as it is for a `let`.
questions.asked: Reading inferred signatures in editor tooltips is daily work, and defaults are the most common source of optional parameters.

questions.q: Why does the call on the last line fail to compile?
choices: `point` is `number[]`, which could hold any number of values
Spread arguments are only allowed for rest parameters in TS
`point` is inferred as `[number, number]`, which is read-only
The array literal is widened to `(number | undefined)[]`
questions.why: Array literals infer as `number[]`, whose length is unknown, so TypeScript cannot prove there are exactly two arguments. Annotate `point` as `[number, number]` or write `[10, 20] as const`; spreading a tuple into fixed parameters is allowed.
questions.asked: It shows whether you understand the array-versus-tuple distinction in inference, which also bites with `Math.max(...xs)` style code.

questions.q: Which assignment does tsc reject?
choices: `c1`, because it ignores the second argument
`c2`, because it declares no parameters at all
`c3`, because it expects a third argument
None of them, since only return types are checked
questions.why: A function with fewer parameters is assignable to a type with more, since ignoring extra arguments is safe; that is why `arr.map((x) => x)` works. A function that needs a third argument would read `undefined`, so `c3` is rejected.
questions.asked: It tests the parameter-count rule behind every callback you pass to `map`, `forEach` or an event API.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this function under `strict`?
choices: Nothing; the function returns `undefined` for `live` at runtime
Nothing unless `noImplicitReturns` is also switched on
An error that `s` is `never` after the `draft` check
An error: the function lacks an ending return statement
questions.why: With a declared return type that does not include `undefined`, falling off the end of the function is an error regardless of `noImplicitReturns`. That flag covers functions without such a return type; here the annotation alone is enough.
questions.asked: Annotating return types on exported functions is a common team rule, and this is one of the bugs it catches.

questions.q: With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled, what happens here?
questions.code:
type Profile = { nickname?: string };
const p: Profile = { nickname: undefined };
choices: It compiles, because `?` always means `string | undefined`
An error: optional properties cannot be set in a literal
It compiles, and the key is removed from the object at runtime
An error: `undefined` is not assignable to `string` here
questions.why: The flag separates "key absent" from "key present with value `undefined`". A `?` property may be missing, but if present it must be a `string`; to allow both, write `nickname?: string | undefined`. It matters for PATCH bodies and spreads, where an explicit `undefined` overwrites a value.
questions.asked: Strong candidates connect it to real bugs, like `{ ...user, ...patch }` wiping a field because the patch held `undefined`.

questions.q: With `noImplicitOverride` on, what does tsc report?
choices: An error: `save` must carry the `override` modifier
An error: base methods must be marked `virtual` to be overridden
Nothing; overriding a method only needs a matching signature
Nothing, but `super.save()` must be called in the override
questions.why: Under `noImplicitOverride`, a subclass member that replaces a base member must say `override`, and `override` on a member with no base counterpart is an error. It catches silent breakage when a base method is renamed. TypeScript has no `virtual` keyword.
questions.asked: It shows familiarity with the stricter flags beyond `strict` and with how renames break class hierarchies.

questions.q: With `verbatimModuleSyntax` on, why does tsc reject line 1 of `app.ts`?
choices: Interfaces cannot be imported, only re-declared per file
The import path needs a `.js` extension under this flag
`User` is only used as a type, so the import must be type-only
Named imports are not allowed; use a default import instead
questions.why: The flag makes emit predictable: imports without `type` are kept verbatim, so importing something that exists only as a type would leave a runtime import of a missing export. Write `import type { User }` or `import { type User }`.
questions.asked: The flag is the modern default for bundler and Node projects, and its error is one of the first new TS users hit.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.8+, with `erasableSyntaxOnly` on, which declaration does tsc reject?
choices: The `type` alias, as aliases need runtime metadata
The `interface`, as it must be converted to a type
The `enum`, as it emits a runtime object
The `declare const`, as it has no initialiser
questions.why: `erasableSyntaxOnly` allows only syntax that can be deleted to leave valid JavaScript, which is what Node 24 type stripping does. Enums, namespaces with values and constructor parameter properties generate code, so they are rejected; types, interfaces and `declare` simply vanish.
questions.asked: With Node running `.ts` files directly, interviewers ask which TypeScript features still need a compiler.

questions.q: You run `node app.ts` on Node 24 and the file contains a type error. What happens?
choices: Node refuses to start and prints the tsc diagnostic
Node strips the types and runs the code without checking
Node prints the type error as a warning, then runs it
Node runs it only when a tsconfig.json sits next to it
questions.why: Node replaces type annotations with whitespace and executes the JavaScript; it never type-checks and ignores tsconfig. You still run `tsc --noEmit` in CI or the editor to catch type errors.
questions.asked: It separates "TypeScript runs" from "TypeScript checked it", which is the whole point of a CI type-check step.

questions.q: What does this constructor do?
choices: Declares two parameters but does not store them anywhere
Declares and assigns two fields, one public and one private
Declares two fields that are both readonly after construction
Creates a public field and a parameter only visible in the body
questions.why: An accessibility modifier on a constructor parameter makes it a parameter property: TypeScript declares the field and emits `this.name = name`. Because it emits code, it is not allowed under `erasableSyntaxOnly`; readonly needs the `readonly` keyword.
questions.asked: The shorthand is everywhere in NestJS and Angular services, so you must read it at a glance.

questions.q: Which line fails to compile?
choices: Line A, because `protected` members are hidden from subclasses
Line B, because `auth` returns a protected value
Line C, because `token` is only visible inside the hierarchy
None, since `protected` is only enforced at runtime
questions.why: `protected` members are accessible within the class and its subclasses but not from outside code. Returning the value from a public method is allowed; the check is on where the member is accessed, and like `private` it is compile-time only.
questions.asked: Access modifiers come up in any OOP-flavoured interview, and TS adds the twist that they vanish at runtime.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the last line?
choices: An error: `total` is a read-only property
Nothing; the assignment is silently ignored at runtime
Nothing; `total` is a plain `number` field on the type
An error: getters cannot be accessed on a new instance
questions.why: A getter without a setter is typed as a read-only property, so assigning to it is a compile error. At runtime in a module (strict mode) the assignment would throw a TypeError rather than being ignored.
questions.asked: Computed properties on models and view-models are common, and knowing TS treats them as readonly avoids pointless casts.

questions.q: Does the last line compile?
choices: No, because `Object.freeze` returns a deeply readonly type
Yes, because `Object.freeze` returns the original mutable type
No, because `host` was inferred as the literal `localhost`
Yes, because the readonly type is only one level deep
questions.why: `Object.freeze` returns `Readonly<T>`, which marks only the top-level properties readonly, matching the runtime behaviour where nested objects stay mutable. `config.port = 1` would fail; nested writes compile and succeed.
questions.asked: Shallow versus deep immutability is a classic follow-up whenever `readonly` or `const` comes up.

questions.q: What is the type of `entries`?
questions.code:
const stock = { apples: 3, pears: 5 };
const entries = Object.entries(stock);
choices: `['apples' | 'pears', number][]`
`(['apples', number] | ['pears', number])[]`
`[string, any][]`
`[string, number][]`
questions.why: Because object types are open (a value may carry extra keys), `Object.entries` returns `string` keys, paired with the union of property value types. It is the same reasoning that makes `Object.keys` return `string[]`.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand why the standard library is deliberately loose about keys, rather than calling it a TS bug.

questions.q: Why does this fail under `strict`, and what is the usual fix?
choices: `reduce` cannot return objects; build the map with `forEach`
`acc` is `{}`, which has no index signature; pass `reduce<Record<string, User>>`
`u` is inferred as `unknown`; annotate it as `(acc, u: User)`
`acc` is `any`, which `strict` forbids; annotate it as `object`
questions.why: The accumulator type is inferred from the initial value `{}`, which cannot be indexed by a string. Supplying the type argument, or typing the seed as `{} as Record<string, User>`, gives `acc` a usable type. `Object.fromEntries` or `Map` are common alternatives.
questions.asked: Grouping and indexing with `reduce` is everyday CRUD code, and this error is one juniors often silence with `any`.

questions.q: What type does TypeScript give `json`, and is it accurate?
questions.code: const json = JSON.stringify(undefined);
choices: `string`, although the value is `undefined`
`string | undefined`, and it is accurate
`never`, since stringifying `undefined` throws
`string`, and the value is the text `'undefined'`
questions.why: The standard library declares `JSON.stringify` as returning `string`, but it returns `undefined` for `undefined`, functions and symbols. It is a deliberate convenience over soundness, so code that stringifies optional values should handle the undefined case itself.
questions.asked: It shows you know the type definitions are hand-written approximations, not a guarantee from the runtime.

questions.q: Why does `const theme: string = localStorage.getItem('theme');` fail under `strict`?
choices: `getItem` returns `any`, which cannot be assigned to `string`
`getItem` returns `unknown` and needs a type guard first
`getItem` returns a `Promise`, so it needs an `await`
`getItem` returns `string | null` for a missing key
questions.why: Web Storage returns `null` when the key is absent, and the DOM types encode that. Handle it with `?? 'light'` or a check; asserting with `!` only hides the first-visit case.
questions.asked: Persisting preferences is a standard take-home feature, and the null case is exactly what first-time users hit.

questions.q: Given a `FormData` from a submitted form, why does `const email: string = data.get('email');` fail?
choices: `get` returns `string[]`, since a field may repeat
`get` returns `FormDataEntryValue | null`: a string, a File, or null
`get` returns `unknown`, since form fields are untyped input
`get` returns `string | undefined` when the field is empty
questions.why: A form field can be a text value or a `File` from a file input, and a missing name gives `null`. Narrow with `typeof v === 'string'` before using it; an empty text input yields an empty string, not `null`.
questions.asked: React 19 form actions hand you `FormData` directly, so reading it safely is now common in interviews.

questions.q: Why does `e.target.value` fail to compile here?
choices: `e` is typed `Event`, and `e.target` is `EventTarget | null`
`e` is typed `any`, which `strict` rejects without annotation
`e.target` is `HTMLInputElement`, but `value` is optional
The listener needs the `InputEvent<HTMLInputElement>` generic
questions.why: The event's target could be any node (events bubble), so the DOM types give `EventTarget | null`. Use the `input` variable you already have, or `e.currentTarget` with a check; `InputEvent` is not generic.
questions.asked: It checks whether you understand why `target` and `currentTarget` differ, not just how to silence the error.

questions.q: What is the type of `port`?
questions.code: const port = process.env.PORT;
choices: `string`, always defined in a Node process
`number`, since ports are numeric
`string | undefined`
`any`, since environment values are untyped
questions.why: `@types/node` types `process.env` as a dictionary of `string | undefined`: every value is text, and any key may be missing. Parse and validate once at startup, e.g. `Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000)` or a schema.
questions.asked: Config handling is where many production crashes start; a strong answer mentions validating env at boot.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this function?
choices: Nothing; `void` means the caller ignores the result
An error: `await` cannot be used in a `void` function
Nothing, but the call sites receive `undefined`
An error: an async function must return a `Promise` type
questions.why: An async function always returns a promise, so its annotated return type must be `Promise<...>`, here `Promise<void>`. Leaving the annotation off would infer that automatically.
questions.asked: It is a quick check that you know `async` changes the return type, which matters when typing callbacks and props.

questions.q: What is the type of `err` in this `.catch` callback under `strict`?
choices: `unknown`, just like a `catch` clause variable
`Error`, since promises reject with errors
`any`, so `err.message` compiles unchecked
`TypeError`, the error `fetch` rejects with
questions.why: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` only affects `try/catch` clauses; the lib types declare the rejection reason as `any`, so the callback parameter is `any`. Annotate it as `(err: unknown)` yourself to get the same safety.
questions.asked: It reveals whether you know where `strict` stops, which matters when an error handler itself crashes.

questions.q: With `lib` set to `["es2020", "dom"]`, why does this fail to compile?
choices: The options argument to `Error` is only typed from `es2022`
`cause` must be an `Error`, and `e` is `unknown`
A caught error cannot be rethrown under `strict`
`Error` needs `new.target` support from `es2022` targets
questions.why: The two-argument `Error` constructor and the `cause` property arrived in ES2022, so the lib typings only include them when `lib` (or `target`) covers `es2022`. `cause` is typed `unknown`, so passing the caught value is fine.
questions.asked: Error chaining with `cause` is the modern way to add context without losing the original stack.

questions.q: What is the type of `c`?
questions.code:
declare const a: { id: number; name: string };
const c = { ...a, id: String(a.id) };
choices: `{ id: string; name: string }`
`{ id: string | number; name: string }`
`{ id: number; name: string }`
An error, since the spread types conflict
questions.why: Spread types follow runtime semantics: later properties overwrite earlier ones, so `id` takes the type of the last assignment. This is how DTO mappers change a field type without a cast.
questions.asked: Mapping entities to DTOs with spreads is routine, and interviewers check you know what type comes out.

questions.q: In React 19 with `@types/react` 19, what is the type of `items`?
choices: `any[]`, since the array literal has no elements
`unknown[]`, the safe default for an empty array
`never[]`, so pushing any item later fails
`undefined[]`, from the empty initial state
questions.why: State type is inferred from the initial value, and an empty array literal in that position infers `never[]`. Pass the type argument, `useState<Todo[]>([])`, whenever the initial value does not show the eventual shape.
questions.asked: It is the most common React-with-TS error, and a quick way to tell who has written typed React.

questions.q: Why does `setUser(loaded)` fail to compile?
choices: `useState(null)` infers the state type as just `null`
State setters cannot be called during render
`loaded` must be spread into a new object first
`useState` needs an initialiser function for objects
questions.why: The state type is inferred from the initial value, which is only `null`. Write `useState<User | null>(null)` so later values fit. Calling a setter during render is a logic issue React reports at runtime, not a type error.
questions.asked: Loading-then-data state is in every React app, so typing it right is a basic expectation.

questions.q: In React 19 types, what does tsc report for `ref.current.focus()`?
choices: Nothing; the ref is typed `HTMLInputElement` once attached
`useRef` requires a second type argument for DOM elements
`current` is readonly, so calling a method on it is rejected
`ref.current` is possibly null, so it needs `?.` or a check
questions.why: In React 19 types, `useRef<T>(null)` returns `RefObject<T | null>`, and the ref really is `null` before mount and after unmount. Use `ref.current?.focus()`; the old mutable-versus-readonly ref split was removed in React 19 types.
questions.asked: Refs to inputs are standard for focus management and accessibility, and the null check reflects the real lifecycle.

questions.q: In `@types/react` 18+, what does tsc report for the usage on the last line?
choices: Nothing; `FC` always includes an optional `children` prop
Nothing; JSX children are not type-checked against props
An error: `Card` takes no props, so it rejects `children`
An error: `FC` components must declare a return type
questions.why: Since React 18 types, `FC` no longer adds `children` implicitly; a component accepts children only if its props say so, e.g. `{ children: ReactNode }` or `PropsWithChildren`. Children are checked like any other prop.
questions.asked: It shows whether your React-TS knowledge predates or follows the React 18 type changes many tutorials still ignore.

questions.q: How should a component that wraps arbitrary content type its `children` prop?
choices: `children: React.ReactNode`
`children: JSX.Element`, which accepts any JSX
`children: React.ReactElement[]`, for lists of elements
`children: string | object`, the two runtime shapes
questions.why: `ReactNode` covers everything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, `null`, `undefined` and booleans. `JSX.Element` accepts only a single element, so plain text or a conditional `null` fails.
questions.asked: Layout and card components take children constantly, so this is a quick screen of practical React-TS.

questions.q: Why does the call on the last line fail, when `o` is not a fresh object literal?
choices: `run` requires at least one property to be present on its argument
Excess property checks apply to every argument, not only to object literals
`retry` is inferred as the literal `3`, which is not assignable to `number`
All of `Options` is optional, and `o` shares none of its properties
questions.why: A type whose properties are all optional is a "weak type", and TypeScript rejects assigning a value that shares no properties with it, which catches typos like `retry`. Excess property checks alone would not fire here, since `o` is not a fresh literal.
questions.asked: Option bags are everywhere, and knowing this rule explains why some typos are caught and others are not.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` in the `else` branch?
choices: `string`, since the readonly array was narrowed away
`readonly string[]`, since `isArray` rejects readonly
`string | readonly string[]`, as nothing was removed
`never`, since every case was handled by the `if`
questions.why: `Array.isArray` is declared as `arg is any[]`, and a `readonly string[]` is not assignable to the mutable `any[]`, so the false branch cannot exclude it. It is a long-standing library typing gap; `typeof x === 'string'` narrows cleanly instead.
questions.asked: It shows you can debug narrowing that "should" work by reading the guard's declared signature.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` inside the `if`?
choices: `unknown[]`, keeping the elements safely unknown
`any[]`, so element access is unchecked from here
`never[]`, since the element type cannot be known
`object`, since arrays are objects at runtime
questions.why: Because the guard is typed `arg is any[]`, narrowing `unknown` with it yields `any[]`, quietly reintroducing `any`. When validating untrusted input, follow it with element checks or annotate as `unknown[]` yourself.
questions.asked: It catches a subtle way `any` leaks back into code that was carefully typed `unknown` at the boundary.

questions.q: What is the type of `body`?
choices: `{ name: string; meta: { v: number } | false }`
`{ name: string; meta?: { v: number } }`
`{ name: string; meta: { v: number } }`
An error, because `false` cannot be spread
questions.why: Spreading `false` adds nothing at runtime, and TypeScript models a spread of `false | { meta }` as an optional property. It is a common idiom for conditional request fields; `includeMeta ? { meta } : {}` gives the same type.
questions.asked: Building request payloads with conditional fields is routine, and the resulting type decides how the API client is checked.

questions.q: Why does the last line fail to compile?
questions.code:
const state = { items: [], loading: false };
state.items.push('apple');
choices: `items` is inferred as `never[]` from the empty literal
`state` is a `const`, so its arrays cannot be changed
`items` is inferred as `readonly unknown[]` by default
`push` is not allowed on arrays inside object literals
questions.why: An empty array inside an object literal has nothing to infer from, so under `strict` it becomes `never[]`, and nothing is assignable to `never`. Annotate the object (e.g. `{ items: [] as string[] }`) or give it a type.
questions.asked: Initial state objects for reducers and stores hit this constantly, and the fix shows you know where inference gets its information.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this declaration?
questions.code: const make: () => { id: number } = () => { id: 1 };
choices: Nothing; the arrow returns the object `{ id: 1 }` as written
An error: object literals need an `as` assertion here
Nothing, but `id` is typed as the literal `1`
An error: the braces are a block, so it returns `void`
questions.why: After `=>`, a `{` starts a function body, so `id: 1` is a label and an expression statement, and the function returns nothing. Wrap the object in parentheses, `() => ({ id: 1 })`; the type annotation is what turns this silent JS bug into a compile error.
questions.asked: It is a classic JS trap that TypeScript catches, and interviewers like candidates who can explain the parse.

questions.q: This compiles under `strict`. What happens at runtime?
choices: It returns `'users/42'`, since class methods are auto-bound
It throws, because `this` is `undefined` in `find`
It returns `'undefined/42'`, reading a global
It returns `undefined`, as `find` exits early
questions.why: Class bodies run in strict mode and methods are not bound, so a detached `find` gets `this === undefined` and reading `this.table` throws a TypeError. TypeScript does not catch it unless the method declares a `this` parameter; arrow-function properties or `.bind` fix it.
questions.asked: Passing methods as callbacks (event handlers, `map`) is where this bites, and TS will not warn you by default.

questions.q: This compiles. What is wrong with the `update` helper?
choices: The result claims `name: string` but holds `undefined` at runtime
Nothing, because spreads skip properties whose value is `undefined`
The `id` can be changed by the patch, which `Partial` should forbid
The spread order is reversed, so the patch is always discarded
questions.why: Spreading copies own properties even when their value is `undefined`, so `name` is overwritten. By default `Partial` allows explicit `undefined`, so tsc accepts it; `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes the call an error. Changing `id` is a design concern, not the type hole here.
questions.asked: PATCH handlers built on `Partial` are common, and this is how "the name went blank" bugs get into production.

questions.q: What does tsc report for `Summary`?
questions.code:
type User = { id: string; name: string };
type Summary = Pick<User, 'id' | 'email'>;
choices: Nothing; `Summary` gets `id` and an `email: unknown`
An error only when a `Summary` value is created
Nothing; the missing key is silently dropped
An error: `'email'` does not satisfy `keyof User`
questions.why: `Pick<T, K>` constrains `K extends keyof T`, so a key that is not on `User` is rejected where the type is written. Note that `Omit` does not have this constraint, so a typo in an `Omit` key compiles.
questions.asked: Deriving DTO types with `Pick` is routine, and it pays to know which utilities check their keys.

questions.q: Which annotation accepts the value `['a', 1]`?
choices: `string[] | number[]`
`(string | number)[]`
`[number, string]`
`Array<string> & Array<number>`
questions.why: `(string | number)[]` is one array whose elements may be either type, so mixing is allowed. `string[] | number[]` means the whole array is all strings or all numbers, and the tuple has the wrong order.
questions.asked: Where the parentheses go changes the meaning completely, and this distinction shows up in API response types.

questions.q: Which line fails to compile?
choices: Line A, because a union cannot be assigned to `string`
Line B, because `string` is wider than the union
Lines A and B, as the two types are unrelated
Neither line, because both hold string values
questions.why: Every member of `'draft' | 'live'` is a string, so assigning the union to `string` is fine. The reverse would allow any text into `status`, so it is rejected; you need a guard or validation to go from `string` to the union.
questions.asked: Assignability direction between literal unions and `string` is the root of many "why won't this compile" questions.

questions.q: What is the type of `total`?
questions.code:
declare const data: any;
const total = data.items.length * 2;
choices: `any`, since it comes from an `any` value
`number`, since `*` always produces a number
`unknown`, since `data.items` is unchecked
An error, since `any` members cannot be read
questions.why: Property access on `any` stays `any`, but the arithmetic operators `*`, `-` and `/` always yield `number`, so `total` looks safely typed even though nothing about `data` was checked. That is how `any` hides behind plausible types.
questions.asked: It shows how `any` can launder itself into ordinary-looking types, which is why reviewers chase it at the source.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
questions.code:
let count: number;
console.log(count + 1);
choices: An error: `count` is used before being assigned
Nothing; `count` is `undefined`, so it logs `NaN`
Nothing; declared numbers default to `0`
An error: `let` declarations must have an initialiser
questions.why: Definite assignment analysis tracks whether a variable has been assigned on every path before it is read. A declaration without an initialiser is fine; reading it before assignment is the error.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know TS tracks assignment, not just types.

questions.q: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on, which loop compiles?
choices: Only A, since the bounds check proves the index is valid
Only B, since `for...of` yields `string` elements
Both, since arrays are exempt from the flag
Neither, since elements are `string | undefined`
questions.why: The flag adds `undefined` to every indexed read, and TypeScript does not relate `i < names.length` to the index, so A fails. Iteration yields the element type directly, so `for...of`, `map` and `forEach` are unaffected.
questions.asked: The flag is increasingly default in new projects, and knowing its ergonomics shows you have lived with it.

questions.q: Under plain `strict`, what are the types of `a` and `b`?
choices: `number` and `number`
`number | undefined` for both
`number` and `number | undefined`
`number | undefined` and `number`
questions.why: Index access returns the element type unless `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is on, while `at()` is declared as returning `T | undefined`. Both are `undefined` for an empty array; only `at` admits it.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know which array APIs are honest about missing elements.

questions.q: In a `.tsx` file, why does `const user = <User>data;` fail to parse?
choices: Angle-bracket assertions were removed in TypeScript 5
The angle brackets are read as a JSX element named `User`
Assertions to interfaces are not allowed in TSX files
`data` must be `unknown` before it can be asserted
questions.why: In TSX, `<User>` starts a JSX element, so the old assertion syntax is ambiguous and disallowed. Use `data as User`, which works in every file type.
questions.asked: It explains why codebases standardise on `as`, and shows you have worked in TSX.

questions.q: Does the last line compile?
choices: No, because `Dog` does not extend `Cat`
Yes, but only because both fields are initialised
No, because class instances are nominally typed
Yes, because the two classes have the same shape
questions.why: TypeScript compares class instance types structurally, so any object with a `name: string` is a `Cat`. Inheritance is not required; adding a `private` or `#private` member is what makes a class behave nominally.
questions.asked: Structural typing surprises people from C# or Java, which is why it is asked in almost every TS screen.

questions.q: Why is the assignment rejected?
choices: Private members are compared by declaration, not by shape
Private members are removed from the type, leaving `{}`
The initial values differ in their declared literal types
Classes with any private member cannot be assigned at all
questions.why: Two types with a `private` or `protected` member are only compatible if that member comes from the same declaration, so `B` is not an `A` despite identical shapes. Subclasses of `A` remain assignable, since they inherit that declaration.
questions.asked: It is the exception to structural typing, and one way to get nominal behaviour for domain types.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the interface?
choices: An error: an interface cannot extend a union type
Nothing; the interface extends whichever member matches
Nothing; the interface becomes a union of labelled shapes
An error: `extends` requires a class or another interface
questions.why: An interface needs a single object type (or intersection of them) with statically known members to extend; a union is not one. Use an intersection instead: `type Labelled = Shape & { label: string }`, which distributes over the members.
questions.asked: It shows you know when you have to reach for `type` and intersections instead of `interface`.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
choices: A duplicate identifier error on the second interface
Nothing; the second declaration replaces the first
An error: property `fontSize` is missing
Nothing; merged interface members become optional
questions.why: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge their members, so `Settings` requires both properties. The same code with two `type` aliases would be a duplicate identifier error; merging is what lets libraries augment types like `Window`.
questions.asked: Declaration merging is the concrete difference between `interface` and `type` that interviewers want you to name.

questions.q: With `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` on, which line fails?
choices: Line A, since declared properties need brackets too
Line B, since `API_URL` comes only from the index signature
Line C, since bracket access is disallowed by the flag
None, since the flag only affects `Record` types
questions.why: The flag forces bracket syntax for keys that exist only via an index signature, so reading a maybe-missing key looks different from reading a declared one. Declared properties keep dot access.
questions.asked: It shows familiarity with the stricter optional flags and the reasoning behind them.

questions.q: What is the difference between `// @ts-expect-error` and `// @ts-ignore`?
choices: `@ts-expect-error` silences only the next line; `@ts-ignore` the whole block
`@ts-expect-error` also stops the line from running at runtime
`@ts-ignore` is removed in TypeScript 5 and only `@ts-expect-error` works
`@ts-expect-error` itself errors if the next line has no error
questions.why: Both suppress errors on the following line, but `@ts-expect-error` reports "unused directive" once the error goes away, so stale suppressions get cleaned up. That also makes it the tool for type-level tests that assert something should not compile.
questions.asked: Teams usually lint for `@ts-expect-error` with a description; knowing why shows care for maintenance.

questions.q: A package has no types, and you add `declare module 'legacy-charts';` to a `.d.ts`. What do its imports become?
choices: Typed as `any`, so every use is unchecked
Typed as `unknown`, so each use needs a type guard first
Typed from the package's JavaScript source by inference
Typed as `never`, so any use is a compile error
questions.why: A shorthand ambient module declaration without a body makes every import from it `any`. It unblocks a build but gives no safety, so a better next step is a small hand-written declaration for the functions you actually use.
questions.asked: Untyped dependencies still happen, and interviewers want to hear the trade-off, not just the workaround.

questions.q: What is an `@types/*` package?
choices: A runtime polyfill that adds type checks to a library
Declarations for a JS library, from the DefinitelyTyped repo
A TypeScript rewrite of a library, maintained by its authors
A tsconfig preset tuned for a particular library
questions.why: Packages like `@types/node` or `@types/express` hold only `.d.ts` files, written by the community in the DefinitelyTyped repo, for libraries that do not ship their own types. They can drift from the library version, so keep their major versions in step.
questions.asked: Everyone installs these; knowing where they come from helps when the types and the runtime disagree.

questions.q: A Vite project builds and runs even though the editor shows type errors. Why?
choices: Vite type-checks only files imported by `index.html`
Vite reports type errors only in production builds
Vite ignores errors unless `strict` is set in tsconfig
Vite strips types per file and never type-checks them
questions.why: Vite (via esbuild or Oxc) removes types file by file for speed and does not run the type checker. That is why templates run `tsc --noEmit` (or `tsc -b`) in the build script and CI.
questions.asked: It separates transpiling from type-checking, a distinction behind many "it built but it is broken" stories.

questions.q: What does `skipLibCheck: true` skip?
choices: Type-checking of all `.d.ts` files, yours included
Type-checking of every file inside `node_modules`
Resolution of `@types` packages not listed in `types`
Checking that imported libraries match their versions
questions.why: It skips checking declaration files for internal consistency, which speeds builds and avoids conflicts between third-party typings. Your `.ts` code is still checked against those declarations, but errors inside your own `.d.ts` files also go unreported.
questions.asked: Nearly every template sets it, and knowing its cost stops you from hiding mistakes in hand-written declarations.

questions.q: A Node project sets `"lib": ["es2022"]` in tsconfig. What happens to `document.title` in a shared helper?
choices: It compiles, since `target` decides the available globals
It fails: `Cannot find name 'document'`
It compiles, since `@types/node` includes the DOM types
It fails only when the helper is run under Node
questions.why: `lib` decides which built-in declarations exist; without `dom`, browser globals like `document` and `window` are unknown. That is a useful guard in server code, and a common surprise when sharing code between front and back end.
questions.asked: It shows you know `lib` and `target` are separate knobs, a frequent tsconfig confusion.

questions.q: With `"types": ["node"]` in tsconfig, a Vitest test using global `describe` stops compiling. Why?
choices: Vitest only exposes globals in `.test.js` files
Global test functions require `isolatedModules`
`@types/node` declares its own conflicting `describe`
A `types` list limits which `@types` globals load
questions.why: By default every package under `node_modules/@types` contributes globals; a `types` array restricts that to the listed ones. Add `vitest/globals` to the list, or import `describe` explicitly from `vitest`.
questions.asked: Global type pollution between test runners and app code is a common monorepo headache.

questions.q: tsconfig maps `"@/*": ["./src/*"]` under `paths`. `tsc` builds, but `node dist/index.js` fails to find `@/db`. Why?
choices: `paths` is not rewritten in the emitted JavaScript
`paths` only works with `moduleResolution: node10`
Node requires the alias to also be in `.npmrc`
tsc only rewrites aliases when `baseUrl` is set
questions.why: tsc leaves import specifiers as written, so `@/db` stays in the emitted JS and Node has no idea what it means. Bundlers read `paths` themselves; for plain Node use package.json `imports` (`#db`) or a build step that rewrites aliases.
questions.asked: It is a very common "works in the editor, fails in production" bug on Node back ends.

questions.q: What does `// @ts-check` at the top of a `.js` file do?
choices: Converts the file to TypeScript during the build
Requires every function in the file to have JSDoc
Enables runtime checks of JSDoc `@param` types
Type-checks the file using inference and JSDoc types
questions.why: The comment opts one JavaScript file into checking by the TypeScript language service (or tsc with `allowJs`), using inference plus JSDoc annotations like `@param {string} name`. Nothing changes at runtime.
questions.asked: Gradual migration questions often start here: how do you get type safety before renaming files?

questions.q: You move an inline `onChange` handler for an `<input>` into a named function. Which parameter type fits it?
choices: `e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`
`e: Event`, the DOM event the browser dispatches
`e: React.InputEvent<string>`, typed by the value
`e: HTMLInputElement`, the element that changed
questions.why: Inline handlers get their type from the `onChange` prop by contextual typing; a standalone function needs it spelt out. `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` types `e.currentTarget.value` and `e.target.value` as `string`. React passes its own synthetic event, not the DOM `Event`.
questions.asked: Forms are most of CRUD UI work, and this is the first annotation everyone needs.

questions.q: Which props type lets a `Button` component accept every native `<button>` attribute plus a `variant`?
choices: `{ variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' } & Partial<HTMLButtonElement>`
`Partial<HTMLElement> & { variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' }`
`{ variant: 'primary' | 'ghost'; [attr: string]: unknown }`
`ComponentProps<'button'> & { variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' }`
questions.why: `ComponentProps<'button'>` is the prop type React accepts for a `<button>`: attributes, event handlers and `ref` in React 19. `HTMLButtonElement` describes the DOM node itself, with methods and read-only fields, not JSX props.
questions.asked: Design-system components wrap native elements all the time, and this is the idiomatic way to keep their full API.

questions.q: Why do many codebases write the context hook like this?
choices: Consumers get `Auth` rather than `Auth | null`, and a missing provider fails loudly
Contexts must default to `null`, or React throws an error at render time
`useContext` cannot be called in components directly, only in custom hooks
The `throw` makes React retry the render once the provider has mounted
questions.why: There is no sensible default `Auth`, so the context is typed nullable; the hook narrows it once, so every caller receives `Auth`, and forgetting the provider gives a clear error instead of `undefined` crashes deep in the tree.
questions.asked: It is the standard typed-context pattern, and interviewers ask why you would not just use a fake default object.

questions.q: What does this props type achieve?
choices: `href` and `onClick` become required props on every usage
A usage may pass `href` or `onClick`, but not both together
`never` removes the props, so neither can be passed at all
It compiles, but TS cannot check which variant is in use
questions.why: Each variant forbids the other's key with an optional `never`, so passing both matches neither member, while each alone matches one. Without the `never` keys, excess property checks on unions are too lenient to reject both.
questions.asked: Mutually exclusive props are a common component-API question, and this is the typed answer.

questions.q: In an Express 5 app with `@types/express`, why does `req.body.emial` compile without complaint?
choices: Express infers `req.body` from the JSON sent by the client
Typos in property names are only reported by ESLint
`req.body` is `unknown`, which permits property reads
`req.body` is typed `any` unless you supply a body type
questions.why: The `Request` type's body parameter defaults to `any`, so every access compiles. Even with `Request<{}, {}, CreateUser>` it is only a claim; validate the body with a schema to get a type you can trust.
questions.asked: API handlers are where untrusted data enters, and interviewers want to hear that types alone do not protect you there.

questions.q: With Zod 4, what is `User`?
choices: `{ email: string; age?: number | undefined }`
`{ email: string; age: number | null }`
`{ email: Email; age?: Int }`, using branded types
`unknown`, until the schema has parsed a value
questions.why: `z.infer` derives the static type from the schema, so the schema is the single source of truth for validation and typing. `.optional()` means the key may be absent or `undefined`; `null` would need `.nullable()`, and refinements like `email` or `int` do not brand the type.
questions.asked: Schema-first typing is the standard answer to "how do you type API input", so knowing what `infer` yields matters.

questions.q: What is the type of `r.data` inside the `if`?
choices: `{ id: string } | undefined`
`unknown`, since `input` was unknown
`{ id: string }`
`any`, since Zod returns loose types
questions.why: `safeParse` returns a discriminated union on `success`, so checking it narrows to the branch with `data`. On the other branch you get `error` instead; `parse` would throw rather than return.
questions.asked: It connects runtime validation with discriminated-union narrowing, two things interviewers like to see together.

questions.q: A handler validates `?page=2` with `z.object({ page: z.number() })` and every request fails. Why?
choices: Query strings are parsed lazily, so `page` is `undefined` at validation
Express converts numeric query values to `bigint`, not `number`
Zod refuses integers unless the schema adds `.int()` to the number type
Query values are strings, so `z.number()` rejects `"2"`; use `z.coerce.number()`
questions.why: URL query parameters always arrive as strings (or arrays of strings). `z.coerce.number()` runs `Number(value)` before validating; add `.int().positive()` so that `"abc"` (NaN) and negatives are still rejected.
questions.asked: Pagination parameters are in every CRUD API, and this is the classic first bug when adding validation.

questions.q: What are `z.input<typeof S>` and `z.output<typeof S>`?
choices: `{ createdAt: Date }` for each, as transforms apply to both
`{ createdAt: string }` and `{ createdAt: Date }`
`{ createdAt: Date }` and `{ createdAt: string }`
`{ createdAt: string }` for each, as transforms are untyped
questions.why: A transform makes the schema accept one shape and produce another: input is what you parse (the JSON string), output is what `parse` returns (a `Date`). `z.infer` is the output type, so a form or client type should use `z.input`.
questions.asked: It shows you understand that one schema can describe two different types, which matters when sharing schemas with a client.

questions.q: What does the generic parameter actually check here?
choices: Only that `User` is a valid type; the body is never checked
That the response body has every property of `User`
That the response `Content-Type` matches `User`
That `/api/me` returns an object rather than an array or null
questions.why: `res.json()` returns `Promise<any>`, which is assignable to `Promise<T>`, so the generic is an assertion with nicer syntax. To make the type true, accept a schema (`getJson(url, UserSchema)`) and validate before returning.
questions.asked: Typed fetch wrappers are a favourite exercise, and the strong answer points out where the lie is.

questions.q: What happens to `import type { User } from './models'` in the emitted JavaScript?
choices: It is kept as an import so that `User` is available at runtime
It is kept, but the bundler removes it later if it is unused
It is converted to a `require` call when targeting CommonJS
It is removed entirely, since it can only refer to types
questions.why: A type-only import is always erased, so it never loads the module or causes a side effect, and it cannot be used as a value. That makes it safe to import types from server-only or heavy modules.
questions.asked: It connects to circular-import and bundle-size questions, and to the `verbatimModuleSyntax` rule.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.5+, what does `isolatedDeclarations` require of a library's exported functions?
choices: That every export lives in its own file with its own `.d.ts`
Explicit types wherever a `.d.ts` would need inference
That exported functions take no generic type parameters
That `declaration` is off, since tools generate the files instead
questions.why: The flag demands that each file's declarations can be emitted without type-checking other files, which usually means explicit return types on exports. That lets fast tools generate `.d.ts` files in parallel, the same idea as `isolatedModules` for JS output.
questions.asked: It shows awareness of how monorepos and libraries speed up builds, and why explicit export types are a team convention.

questions.q: In a monorepo, what do `composite: true` and project `references` give you?
choices: Per-package builds that `tsc -b` orders and skips when unchanged
A single program that type-checks every package together as one unit
Automatic publishing of each package to the npm registry
Shared `node_modules` between packages without a workspace tool
questions.why: Each referenced project builds separately, emitting `.d.ts` files and a `.tsbuildinfo`; `tsc -b` builds them in dependency order and skips up-to-date ones. Consumers type-check against the declarations rather than re-checking the source.
questions.asked: Build times in a TS monorepo are a real mid-level concern, and references are the built-in answer.

questions.q: tsconfig has `outDir: "dist"` and no `rootDir`. After adding `scripts/seed.ts` next to `src/`, the output moves from `dist/index.js` to `dist/src/index.js`. Why?
choices: tsc always mirrors the path from `package.json` into `outDir`
Scripts are compiled first, so they claim the top of `dist`
`outDir` is ignored when a file lives outside the `src` folder
Without `rootDir`, output mirrors the common root of all inputs
questions.why: When `rootDir` is not set, tsc uses the longest common directory of the input files; including a file outside `src` raises that root to the project folder. Set `rootDir: "src"` (and keep scripts in a separate config) so the layout stays stable.
questions.asked: It is a classic "the start script broke after an unrelated change" debugging story.

questions.q: Which setting lets you write `import config from './config.json'` with a typed result?
choices: `resolveJsonModule`, which types the file from its content
`allowJs`, which treats JSON as JavaScript source
`esModuleInterop`, which adds a default export to JSON
`types: ["json"]`, which adds a global JSON module declaration
questions.why: With `resolveJsonModule`, tsc reads the JSON file and infers its type (strings widen to `string`). On Node ESM you also need an import attribute: `with { type: 'json' }`.
questions.asked: Importing config and fixtures is common, and it shows you know the tsconfig flags beyond `strict`.

questions.q: Without `esModuleInterop`, why can `import express from 'express'` fail to type-check?
choices: Express is ESM-only and has no default export at all
Express types are only visible through `import type`
Default imports are disallowed when `strict` is enabled
Express is CommonJS (`export =`), with no default export
questions.why: CommonJS modules export a single `module.exports` value, declared with `export =`. The interop flag (on by default in modern configs, together with `allowSyntheticDefaultImports`) lets you treat it as a default export and emits helpers so it works at runtime.
questions.asked: Mixed CJS and ESM is still daily life on Node, and this is its most common TypeScript symptom.

questions.q: What does `"strict": true` do in tsconfig?
choices: Enables a family of checks, such as `strictNullChecks`
Enables runtime checks that throw when a value has the wrong type
Makes tsc treat all warnings as errors, including unused variables
Turns on JavaScript strict mode, which is its only effect
questions.why: `strict` is shorthand for several checks, including `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes` and `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, and new ones join it in later versions. You can still turn one off individually. Unused-variable checks are separate flags.
questions.asked: Knowing that `strict` grows with new releases explains why upgrades sometimes introduce new errors.

questions.q: With `noUnusedParameters` on, how do you keep an Express error middleware's unused `next` parameter?
choices: Add `// @ts-ignore` above the function declaration
Rename it with a leading underscore, such as `_next`
Mark it optional with `next?`, which exempts it
Remove it, since Express identifies middleware by its name
questions.why: Parameters whose names start with `_` are exempt from the unused check. Removing it is wrong for Express: error middleware is recognised by having four parameters, so the position must stay.
questions.asked: It combines a TS flag with an Express quirk, both of which catch people in real code.

questions.q: The `User` entity has `passwordHash`. Which type best describes the user your API returns?
choices: `Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>`, built by an explicit mapper
`User`, and the handler deletes the field before sending
`Partial<User>`, so any field may be left out of the reply
`Record<string, unknown>`, as responses are just JSON
questions.why: A separate response type states what leaves the server, and a mapper that builds it field by field means a new secret column is not leaked by accident. Types do not strip properties at runtime, so returning a full `User` typed as the smaller type would still send the hash.
questions.asked: DTOs versus entities is a core CRUD design question, and the runtime-versus-type distinction is the key insight.

questions.q: A React front end and a Node API live in one repo. What is the usual way to share request and response types?
choices: Copy the types into each app so they can change independently
Generate types from the database at build time in each app
Import the API's source files directly from the front end with relative paths
A shared workspace package, ideally holding schemas the types come from
questions.why: A shared package (in npm, pnpm or Yarn workspaces) keeps one definition, and exporting schemas lets both sides validate as well as type. Relative imports into the API drag server code and dependencies into the client bundle; copies drift.
questions.asked: Full-stack TS roles ask this to see whether you have maintained a contract between two apps.

questions.q: A back end publishes an OpenAPI spec. What is the main benefit of generating client types from it (e.g. with `openapi-typescript`)?
choices: Client types track the spec, so API changes break the build
Responses are validated at runtime without any schema library
The generated client works offline by mocking every endpoint
The front end can skip handling error responses entirely
questions.why: Generated types keep the client aligned with the spec, and regenerating after an API change turns a renamed field into compile errors. They are still static types: runtime validation or contract tests are needed if the server can drift from its spec.
questions.asked: Contract-first APIs are common across teams and languages, e.g. an ASP.NET back end with a TS front end.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.5+, what is the type of `values`?
choices: An error: `value` does not exist on a rejected result
`unknown[]`, since `allSettled` hides the value type
`(number | undefined)[]`, from the rejected entries
`number[]`, as the filter infers a type predicate
questions.why: Since 5.5, a callback like `(r) => r.status === 'fulfilled'` that narrows its parameter is inferred as a type predicate, so `filter` returns `PromiseFulfilledResult<number>[]`. Before 5.5 you needed an explicit `r is PromiseFulfilledResult<number>` annotation.
questions.asked: Batch operations with `allSettled` are common, and knowing when TS infers predicates saves you boilerplate.

questions.q: With `@types/express`, what is the type of `req.params.id` in this handler?
choices: `string`, parsed from the `:id` in the route pattern
`string | undefined`, since route params may be missing
`number`, since the segment looks like an identifier
`any`, since Express has no types for route params
questions.why: The Express types parse the path literal with template literal types, so `'/users/:id'` gives `params: { id: string }`. Parameters are always strings; convert and validate them yourself, and a typo like `req.params.userId` becomes a compile error.
questions.asked: It shows you know what the framework types give you for free and what still needs validation.

questions.q: Which dispatch does tsc reject?
choices: Line A, since every action needs a payload
Line B, since `add` requires `text`
Line C, since `text` is not on every member
None, since `type` is all TS checks
questions.why: The object literal must match one member of the union; with `type: 'add'` only the member requiring `text` fits. This is why typed reducers catch missing payloads at the call site.
questions.asked: Typed reducer actions are a staple of React-TS interviews, and this is the payoff they bring.

questions.q: Which class declaration is valid?
choices: `class Repo extends Base, Other {}`
`class Repo implements Base extends Other {}`
`class Repo extends Base implements Saves, Loads {}`
`class Repo implements Saves, extends Base {}` with `save` defined
questions.why: A class extends at most one class and may implement any number of interfaces, with `extends` written first. `implements` only checks the shape; it does not inherit any code.
questions.asked: A basic OOP check, often followed by "then how would you share behaviour between two classes?"

questions.q: Does the call on the last line compile?
choices: Yes, because a mutable array can be passed as a readonly one
No, because a mutable array is not a `readonly number[]`
No, because `reduce` is not declared on `readonly` array types
Yes, but only after spreading it into a new array
questions.why: Mutable arrays have every method readonly arrays have, so they are assignable to them; the parameter type just promises the function will not mutate the argument. The reverse, passing a readonly array to a `number[]` parameter, is the direction that fails.
questions.asked: Typing parameters as readonly is a cheap way to document intent, and interviewers check you know it does not burden callers.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` inside the `if`?
choices: `never`, since `in` ignores keys that are optional
`Email | Sms`, since `subject` is optional
`Email & { subject: string }`, a refined type
`Email`, since only `Email` declares `subject`
questions.why: The `in` check keeps union members that declare the key, even as optional, and drops those that do not. It does not make `subject` defined; it only tells you the key exists on the object.
questions.asked: The `in` operator is the go-to guard for unions without a shared discriminant, and its handling of optional keys is a common follow-up.

questions.q: What is `u` in the `getLabel` callback?
choices: `unknown`, until you pass `<Select<User>>` explicitly
`User`, inferred from the `options` prop
`any`, since JSX props are not generic
`T`, left unresolved inside the callback
questions.why: Generic components infer their type parameters from props just like function calls, so `options={users}` fixes `T` as `User` and the callback is contextually typed. Explicit JSX type arguments exist but are rarely needed.
questions.asked: Reusable tables and selects are generic components, and interviewers probe whether you can type one.

questions.q: Why does tsc reject this effect?
choices: `useEffect` callbacks may not call state setters directly
The dependency array must also list `fetch` and `setTodos`
`await` is not allowed inside React hook callbacks
An async function returns a Promise, not a cleanup or nothing
questions.why: The effect callback must return `void` or a cleanup function, and an async function always returns a promise, which React would try to call on cleanup. Define an async function inside the effect and call it, ideally with an `AbortController` for cleanup.
questions.asked: It is one of the first React-TS errors people hit, and the fix leads naturally into race conditions and cleanup.

questions.q: What is the advantage of parsing `process.env` with a schema at startup?
choices: It makes `process.env` values encrypted in memory at runtime
The app fails at boot on bad config, and `env` is fully typed
It lets TypeScript read the `.env` file during compilation
It removes the need to set environment variables in production
questions.why: Validating once turns scattered `string | undefined` reads into one typed object with real numbers and defaults, and a missing variable crashes the deploy immediately instead of on the first request that needs it. The types come from the schema, not from the environment.
questions.asked: Fail-fast config is a mark of production experience and appears in most back-end interviews.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the last line?
choices: Nothing; subtracting two dates yields the gap in milliseconds
An error: arithmetic needs `number`, `bigint` or `any` operands
Nothing, but `ms` is typed `Date` rather than `number`
An error: `Date` objects can only be compared with `<`
questions.why: JavaScript coerces dates to numbers here, but TypeScript only allows arithmetic on number-like types. Write `end.getTime() - start.getTime()`; relational comparisons like `start < end` are allowed.
questions.asked: Date maths comes up in every booking or reporting feature, and TS pushes you to the explicit form.

questions.q: Which line fails to compile?
questions.code:
const qty = '5';
const a = qty + 2;   // A
const b = qty * 2;   // B
const c = +qty * 2;  // C
choices: Line A, because `+` cannot mix strings and numbers
Line B, because `*` needs a number on the left
Line C, because unary `+` is not allowed on strings
None, because JavaScript coerces all three
questions.why: `+` with a string is concatenation, which TS allows (giving `'52'`). Other arithmetic operators require number-like operands, so `qty * 2` is an error even though JS would coerce it. Unary `+` is an explicit conversion and gives `number`.
questions.asked: Form inputs are strings, and this is where TS forces the conversion JS would do silently.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
choices: Nothing; the comparison is simply always `false`
An error: the types `string` and `number` have no overlap
Nothing, since `===` compares values of any type
An error: `id` must be converted with `Number(id)` first
questions.why: TypeScript flags comparisons between types that can never be equal, because they are almost always bugs, such as an ID that is a number in one layer and a string in another. `==` gets the same check.
questions.asked: ID type mismatches between API, database and UI are common; this is how TS surfaces them.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this catch clause?
choices: An error: a catch variable may only be annotated `any` or `unknown`
Nothing; the annotation narrows `err` to `Error`
Nothing, but a non-Error throw becomes `undefined`
An error: `await` is not allowed inside `try`
questions.why: Anything can be thrown, so TypeScript will not let you claim the catch variable is an `Error`. Leave it as `unknown` and narrow with `err instanceof Error`.
questions.asked: Error handling code is where type assumptions crash hardest, so interviewers check you do not assume `Error`.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the last line?
choices: Nothing; statics are also visible on each instance
An error: static fields cannot be changed
Nothing, but it logs `undefined` at runtime
An error: `count` does not exist on type `User`
questions.why: Static members live on the constructor, `User.count`, not on instances, so the instance type has no `count`. The class name in a type position means the instance type; the static side is `typeof User`.
questions.asked: A simple check of the instance versus static split, which trips up people coming from other languages.

questions.q: A React component file contains JSX. Which extension must it use for tsc to accept the JSX?
choices: `.ts`
`.tsx`
`.jsx.ts`
`.d.tsx`
questions.why: TypeScript only parses JSX in `.tsx` files, since `<T>` in `.ts` means a type assertion. The `jsx` compiler option then controls how it is emitted (`react-jsx` for the modern runtime).
questions.asked: A warm-up that often leads into why `<T>` assertions are not used in TSX.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
questions.code: const range: [number, number] = [1, 5, 10];
choices: An error: source has 3 elements but target allows only 2
Nothing; extra elements are ignored by tuples
Nothing; the type widens to `number[]`
An error: tuple types cannot be created from array literals
questions.why: A fixed tuple type records its length, so a literal with more elements is rejected. Optional (`[number, number?]`) and rest (`[number, ...number[]]`) elements exist when the length varies.
questions.asked: Tuples model pairs like ranges and coordinates, and knowing they check length is basic fluency.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the last line?
choices: Nothing; objects can gain properties at runtime
An error only because `p` was declared with `const`
Nothing; `p` widens to `Point & { z: number }`
An error: property `z` does not exist on type `Point`
questions.why: An object type lists the properties you may use, and adding one later is rejected even though JavaScript allows it. Declare the full shape up front, or use a `Map`/`Record` for dynamic keys. `const` only stops reassigning `p` itself.
questions.asked: Building objects incrementally is a JS habit TypeScript pushes back on, so it comes up early.

questions.q: How do you annotate the return type of an arrow function?
choices: `const f = (n: number): string => String(n);`
`const f: string = (n: number) => String(n);`
`const f = (n: number) => string: String(n);`
`const f = <string>(n: number) => String(n);`
questions.why: The return annotation goes after the parameter list and before the arrow. Annotating the variable as `string` claims the function is a string, and `<string>` before the parameters declares a type parameter named `string`, not a return type.
questions.asked: Basic syntax fluency; teams often require return types on exported functions.

questions.q: What does tsc report?
choices: Nothing; `delete` works on any property
An error: parameters cannot be modified in place
Nothing, but `u` becomes `Partial<User>` afterwards
An error: the operand of `delete` must be optional
questions.why: Under `strictNullChecks`, deleting a required property would leave a value that no longer matches its type, so it is rejected. Build a new object without the field, e.g. `const { name, ...rest } = u`.
questions.asked: Removing sensitive fields before a response is common, and TS steers you to non-mutating code.

questions.q: Why does this compile, and what is the risk?
questions.code:
const labels: Record<string, string> = { title: 'Title', body: 'Body' };
const l = labels.tittle;
choices: Compiles because `labels` has an index signature, so typos are allowed
Compiles because `Record` checks keys only when the object is created
Compiles because property typos are warnings, not errors, in TS
Compiles because `tittle` is inferred as a new optional property
questions.why: With `string` keys, every property name is valid and typed `string`, so a misspelt key compiles and yields `undefined`. Using a key union, `Record<'title' | 'body', string>`, or `satisfies` keeps the literal keys checked.
questions.asked: Translation and config maps are often typed this way, and the silent-typo risk is what a reviewer spots.

questions.q: What is the type of `user.age` on the `return` line?
choices: `number | null`, since only locals can be narrowed
`number`, since the property access path was narrowed
`any`, since narrowing a property widens it
`never`, since `null` is also an object
questions.why: Narrowing works on reference paths like `user.age`, not only on plain variables, as long as nothing in between could reassign it. It does not narrow `user` itself; a discriminated union is needed for that.
questions.asked: Checking nullable fields in place is common, and knowing it works avoids needless local copies.

questions.q: What is the type of `u` inside the `if`?
choices: `User | undefined`, as `?.` does not narrow
`never`, since `address` is optional
`{ address: { city: string } }`, with `address` required
`User`, as a truthy chain implies `u` is defined
questions.why: If `u?.address` is truthy, `u` cannot be `undefined`, so TS narrows `u` to `User`, and `u.address` to the defined object too. The object type itself is not rewritten to make `address` required.
questions.asked: Optional chaining in conditions is idiomatic, and knowing it narrows the whole chain saves redundant checks.

questions.q: Why does the last line fail to compile?
choices: The inferred return type widens `status` to `string`
`ok()` returns an object, but `Res` needs a class instance
`data` is optional in `Res`, but required in the result
Unions cannot be the declared type of a `const`
questions.why: Without contextual type, object literal properties widen, so `ok` returns `{ status: string; data: string }`, which matches neither member. Annotate the function's return type as `Res` (or use `as const`) so the literal is kept.
questions.asked: It explains why explicit return types on functions that build union values save a lot of confusion.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this condition?
choices: Nothing; it checks whether `save` exists on the object
An error: class methods cannot be used in boolean contexts
Nothing; methods are converted to their return value
An error: the condition is always true; was a call intended?
questions.why: Since the method is not optional, testing it for truthiness is always true and almost certainly a missing `()`. TypeScript reports it, unless the function is optional or used inside the block.
questions.asked: A forgotten call is a sneaky bug, and it shows TS catches logic errors, not only type mismatches.

questions.q: This compiles. What does it log?
questions.code:
const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ann' };
console.log(`Hello ${user}`);
choices: `Hello Ann`, via the object's `name`
`Hello [object Object]`
`Hello {"id":1,"name":"Ann"}`
Nothing; it throws a TypeError
questions.why: Template literals call `String()` on each value, and TypeScript accepts any type there. The typescript-eslint rule `restrict-template-expressions` is what catches objects slipping into strings.
questions.asked: It shows where the compiler stops and linting takes over, a distinction good teams rely on.

questions.q: In a project with both `dom` and `@types/node`, why does `const t: number = setTimeout(tick, 100);` fail?
choices: Node's overload wins and returns a `Timeout` object
`setTimeout` returns `void` in both environments
`setTimeout` returns `Promise<number>` in Node 24
A callback must be an arrow function, not a name
questions.why: With Node types loaded, the global `setTimeout` resolves to Node's declaration, which returns `NodeJS.Timeout`. Portable code types the handle as `ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>`.
questions.asked: Shared front-end and back-end code hits this constantly, and the portable annotation is a telling answer.

questions.q: `tsc` prints type errors, yet the `dist` folder is updated with new JavaScript. Why?
choices: Type errors in `.ts` files are only warnings by default
Only files without errors are written to `outDir`
tsc emits the last successful build from its cache
`noEmitOnError` is off by default, so tsc emits anyway
questions.why: Types do not affect emit, so tsc writes output even when checking fails unless `noEmitOnError` is set. The exit code is still non-zero, which is what CI should rely on.
questions.asked: It shows you understand emit and checking are separate, which matters for build scripts and deploys.

questions.q: In React 19, what is the type of `user`?
choices: `User | undefined`, as no initial value was passed
`User`, since the type argument was given
`User | null`, the default for empty state
An error: `useState` requires an argument
questions.why: Calling `useState` with no initial value uses an overload that adds `undefined`, matching the runtime. Pick `undefined` or an explicit `null` deliberately and handle it when rendering.
questions.asked: Typing loading state is routine, and it reveals whether you know how overloads shape hook types.

questions.q: What does `Object.values(Status)` return at runtime?
questions.code:
enum Status { Active, Closed }
const all = Object.values(Status);
choices: `['Active', 'Closed']`
`['Active', 'Closed', 0, 1]`
`[{ Active: 0 }, { Closed: 1 }]`
questions.why: Numeric enums compile to an object with reverse mappings, so it holds both `Active: 0` and `0: 'Active'`. Iterating it for a dropdown yields names and numbers; string enums or `as const` objects avoid the surprise.
questions.asked: Building select options from an enum is common, and this runtime shape causes duplicated entries.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.6+, what does tsc report for this function?
choices: Nothing; the regex is tested against `s` implicitly
An error: a regex literal must be assigned first
Nothing, but the function always returns `false`
An error: this kind of expression is always truthy
questions.why: TS 5.6 reports conditions that are syntactically always truthy or always nullish, such as a regex literal, an object literal or an arrow function. Here the author forgot `.test(s)`; at runtime the function would always return `true`.
questions.asked: It shows you keep up with how newer releases catch logic bugs, not only type mismatches.

questions.q: With `target: es2022` (so class fields use define semantics), what does tsc report?
choices: Nothing; parameter properties are assigned before fields
An error: `amount` is used before it is initialised
Nothing, but `doubled` ends up as `NaN` at runtime
An error: field initialisers cannot reference `this`
