questions.why: With native class fields, field initialisers run before the constructor body that assigns parameter properties, so `this.amount` is still `undefined`. TS reports it; compute `doubled` in the constructor or as a getter.
questions.asked: Field initialisation order changed with standard class fields, and it breaks code migrated from older targets.

questions.q: This compiles. What happens at runtime?
choices: It throws, because the clone is a plain object
It returns `'£5.00'`, as the clone is a `Money`
It throws, because class instances cannot be cloned
It returns `'£NaN'`, as `cents` is lost
questions.why: `structuredClone` copies data but not the prototype, so the copy has `cents` but no `format`. Its signature returns the input type `T`, so TS believes the method exists. The same applies after a JSON round-trip.
questions.asked: Class instances crossing clone, cache or JSON boundaries is a real source of "is not a function" errors.

questions.q: A project compiles to `target: es5`. Why can `err instanceof NotFoundError` be false for a thrown `NotFoundError`?
choices: ES5 has no `instanceof` operator, so TS emits a shim
`instanceof` compares names, and ES5 minifies them
Custom errors are thrown as strings under ES5
The ES5 `Error` subclass loses its prototype chain
questions.why: Down-levelled `extends Error` calls `Error` as a function, which returns a new object with `Error.prototype`, so the subclass prototype is lost. The old fix is `Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype)`; targeting ES2015+ avoids it.
questions.asked: Legacy build targets still exist, and this bug explains a line of boilerplate seen in older codebases.

questions.q: What does the constraint `T extends {}` exclude?
choices: `null` and `undefined`, but no other values
Primitives such as strings and numbers
Arrays and functions, as they are not plain objects
Nothing; `{}` accepts every possible value
questions.why: `{}` means "any non-nullish value", so strings and numbers qualify, but `null` and `undefined` do not. It is how `NonNullable<T>` is defined (`T & {}`); use `object` to rule out primitives.
questions.asked: The `{}` versus `object` versus `unknown` distinction trips up many, and shows up in library signatures.

questions.q: An Express handler does `res.json(user)` where `user` is an instance with `private passwordHash`. Is the hash sent?
choices: No; `private` fields are skipped by `JSON.stringify`
Yes, but only when `strict` is turned off in tsconfig
No; TypeScript strips private fields from the emitted class
Yes; `private` is compile-time only and the field is serialised
questions.why: TS `private` only restricts access in type-checked code; the property is an ordinary own property at runtime, so it serialises. `#passwordHash` would not be serialised, but the real fix is mapping to an explicit response type.
questions.asked: Leaking secrets in API responses is a real security bug, and it tests whether you know what `private` means.

questions.q: This compiles under `strict`. What does it show about `readonly`?
choices: Readonly properties are assignable to mutable ones, so it leaks
Readonly objects are copied when assigned to a mutable type
The last line throws at runtime, as `count` is frozen
The assignment fails at runtime due to the readonly flag
questions.why: For object properties, `readonly` does not affect assignability, so an alias without it can mutate the "readonly" object. It is a compile-time promise about one reference, not a runtime freeze; `readonly` arrays, by contrast, are not assignable to mutable arrays.
questions.asked: It separates people who think `readonly` is immutability from those who know it is a view-level hint.

questions.q: Why do teams add typescript-eslint with type-aware rules on top of `tsc --strict`?
choices: tsc does not check `.tsx` files unless ESLint runs first
Rules like `no-floating-promises` catch bugs tsc allows
ESLint replaces tsc, so the build no longer needs it
Strict mode only applies once ESLint has approved a file
questions.why: tsc checks types, not intent: an un-awaited promise, a misused `async` callback or an object in a template string are all type-correct. Type-aware lint rules use the checker to flag those patterns.
questions.asked: It shows you know the limits of the compiler and how teams cover them in CI.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.2+, what does `using` do in this function?
choices: It imports `conn` into the module scope once the function returns
It marks `conn` readonly so it cannot be reassigned in the body
It retries `pool.connect()` until a connection is available
It disposes `conn` via `Symbol.asyncDispose` when the scope exits
questions.why: Explicit resource management calls the object's `[Symbol.asyncDispose]` (or `[Symbol.dispose]` for `using`) when the block exits, even on a throw, replacing `try/finally` cleanup. The object must declare that method for tsc to accept it.
questions.asked: Releasing connections and file handles reliably is a real back-end concern, and `using` is the new idiom.

questions.q: Which statement about TypeScript enums is accurate?
choices: String enums allow assigning any matching string literal
Enums are the only syntax that `erasableSyntaxOnly` rejects
A `const enum` is inlined, but breaks with `isolatedModules` across files
Numeric enums prevent any plain number from being assigned
questions.why: `const enum` members are inlined at use sites, which needs type information from other files, so single-file transpilers cannot do it and `isolatedModules` restricts it. String enums reject raw literals, and namespaces or parameter properties are also non-erasable.
questions.asked: Enums still appear in older codebases, and knowing the tooling constraints informs whether to migrate.

questions.q: You receive `{ "total": "19.99" }` from an API typed as `{ total: number }`. What does `order.total + 5` evaluate to?
choices: `24.99`, as TypeScript converts it to the declared type
A runtime TypeError from the type mismatch
A compile error, since the JSON does not match
`"19.995"`, since the runtime value is a string
questions.why: Types are erased and never convert values, so a string that the type calls a number concatenates. Decimal amounts are often sent as strings; validate with a schema (`z.coerce.number()` or a decimal type) at the boundary.
questions.asked: It is the plainest demonstration that types describe expectations, not data, which interviewers want to hear.
